# package-skill-generator popularity-sample test log

Started 2026-09-09. Goal: determine where there is a serious need for
an MCP other than the base sublime-mcp -- i.e. which real, popular
Sublime Text packages genuinely require their own dedicated
integration (the way Debugger and LSP got real
`debugger-control`/`lsp-control` skills), versus ones sublime-mcp's
generic "discover -> read source -> call directly" already covers
completely. A package nobody uses isn't worth building anything
dedicated for regardless of the answer, so candidates are selected by
real install-count ranking from `packagecontrol.io/browse/popular.json`,
not by unfiltered random draw from the full package corpus.

**Rolled back 2026-09-14**: entries for packages 24+ (HypnotoadSVN
onward) were selected by pure random sampling against a 4442-entry
`clone_list.tsv` corpus instead of the install-count criteria above --
that drift produced a long run of low-usage, unmaintained "dog"
packages irrelevant to the actual question. Those entries were deleted,
not archived. Resuming from package 23 (AdvancedNewFile), next pick by
real packagecontrol.io popularity rank.

**Standing methodology rule (added day 5, applies retroactively to every
entry below that claims "no error occurred"): `get_console(mode="captured")`
is NOT valid for verifying the absence of a crash.** It is explicitly
non-invasive and incomplete -- it can silently drop lines, including
tracebacks, and will falsely report a clean run. It produced exactly this
false negative on SublimeLinter-pyflakes (package #37): a run that had
actually crashed 4/4 times looked crash-free under `mode="captured"` and
only showed the real traceback under `mode="auto"`/`"visible"` (the
complete capture). Any "did this actually work / did this actually
crash" check must use the complete capture, never the incomplete one.
Earlier entries in this log that checked console output for absence of
errors were not necessarily using the complete capture and have not been
retroactively re-verified against this rule -- treat any of them as
provisional if the distinction matters for a specific decision.

**Second standing methodology rule (added closing this campaign, from
the EditorConfig #39 trim-whitespace false finding): an edit-then-save
round trip must verify the edit landed where intended before trusting
the save result.** Inserting a test marker *after* the region actually
being tested (e.g. after trailing whitespace, when testing whether
trailing whitespace gets trimmed) silently changes what the test is
measuring -- the marker makes prior content interior, not trailing, so
there is nothing left for the feature under test to act on. This
produced a real false "bug" report in the same session it was found.
Print/verify the actual buffer content immediately after making a test
edit, before saving and checking the result.

Packages already tested before this log existed (do not re-pick):
- OpenFileOverSSH (AncientRoman/SublimeOpenFileOverSSH) -- 1/1 commands,
  100% coverage, skill verified end-to-end against a real SSH target.
- Debugger (SublimeText's Debugger package) -- ~40% coverage documented
  (mechanical action table + state/breakpoints/control), deep tools
  (variables/callstacks/evaluate) not investigated.
- LSP (via LSP-pyright) -- hover/definition/references/etc. bridge
  documented and verified; found a live bug in lsp-mcp's own can_handle()
  call during testing.

## Log format

Each entry: date, package name + repo, install method, coverage
assessment (X/Y real commands captured), whether a skill file was
generated and where, whether it was verified against a live action or
only read-verified, and any real gotcha/bug found. Be honest about
partial or failed cases -- this log exists to find where the thesis
breaks, not to pad a success count.

## Entries

### Day 1 (2026-09-09): Notr

Repo: cepthomas/Notr (2.2MB, actively maintained, pushed 2026-08-03).
17 commands, 5 settings, 1744 lines across 3 source files (notr.py,
sbot_common.py, table.py). Picked specifically because the user pushed
back hard on the thesis after looking at ~5 packages themselves and
being "astounded at the craftsmanship" -- this needed to be a real,
substantial package, not another trivial one.

**Result: thesis holds, but with a real, concrete exception found.**

- The user independently hit a live "no project selected" warning after
  install -- correctly predicting the package's real behavior before I'd
  even read the source. Notr keeps module-level state (`_current_project`)
  that gates almost everything.
- Reading the source (not just introspection -- introspection alone gave
  no hint of this precondition) found that the actual onboarding command,
  `notr_open_project`, has a `run()` with ZERO arguments -- it only opens
  an interactive `quick_panel` for a human to click. **There is no way to
  drive this specific command via `run_command` with args, period.** This
  is a real, if narrow, falsification of "run_command args are always
  enough."
- However, the deeper escape hatch -- reaching into the live module via
  `sys.modules` and calling `_open_project()`/`_process_all_files()`
  directly, the same pattern used for Debugger and LSP -- worked
  perfectly. No dedicated MCP server was needed; `eval_python` alone
  handled the one case `run_command` couldn't.
- Verified end-to-end: opened the package's own shipped demo project
  (extracted from the .sublime-package zip, paths rewritten since it
  assumed a loose install), state initialized correctly, then the
  standard `notr_dump` command via plain `run_command` returned real,
  correct parsed content.
- Skill written: ~/.claude/skills/notr-control/SKILL.md.

### Day 1, second package (2026-09-09): Helium

Repo: SublimeText/Helium (6.5MB, actively maintained, pushed 2026-08-06).
"Let Sublime Text talk with Jupyter" -- vendors the entire real
`jupyter_client` library (kernel discovery, connection files, session
management) plus `traitlets` and `ipython_genutils` directly into the
plugin. By far the most structurally complex package looked at so far --
a real test of whether the thesis holds against genuine infrastructure,
not just a feature-rich but self-contained package like Notr.

**Result: could not be tested at all -- a different kind of finding.**

The plugin's own module failed to import entirely:
`ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'zmq'`. Helium vendors the pure-
Python parts of the Jupyter client stack but not `pyzmq`, which needs a
compiled binary matching Sublime's embedded Python 3.8 build exactly --
not something that can be vendored as plain source, and not present in
this Sublime install. Confirmed via the real traceback from
`get_console()`, not guessed.

This is a genuine boundary case for the whole thesis, not a point for or
against it: when the underlying package can't even load, no control
technique applies -- not `run_command`, not `eval_python`, not a
dedicated MCP server either. The question "can you control this package
without a dedicated MCP" doesn't arise until the package actually works
in the first place. Did not attempt to install `pyzmq` to unblock this --
the user has been burned by Python environment installs before and asked
not to go there. Package fully uninstalled afterward (settings entry +
`.sublime-package` file removed directly, matching the debugger-mcp/
lsp-mcp removal method from earlier tonight) rather than left in a
broken, non-functional state.

Also hit a small, separate discovery mid-cleanup: Package Control's own
`remove_package` command does not accept `package` or `package_name` as
a kwarg when called via `run_command` (`TypeError: run() got an
unexpected keyword argument`) -- it's evidently UI-only (shows its own
picker) like several other commands found tonight. Worth remembering for
future cleanup: go straight to the settings-file + file-deletion method
instead of guessing at `run_command` args for it.

### Day 1, third package (2026-09-09): OpenUri

Repo: jfcherng-sublime/ST-OpenUri (744KB, actively maintained). Real,
well-organized subpackage structure (`plugin/commands/`, `plugin/ui/`,
`plugin/libs/`). Picked deliberately as a control case after two packages
in a row that each had a real complication, to check the thesis isn't
just "everything has a gotcha."

**Result: clean success, no gotchas at all.** 7 commands, all plain
TextCommands, all callable via standard `run_command` on the first try.
Verified live: opened a test file with two real URLs, ran
`copy_uri_from_view`, both came back exactly right via the OS clipboard.
No eval_python needed, no stateful preconditions, no UI-only blocking
commands. Skill written: ~/.claude/skills/openuri-control/SKILL.md.

**Takeaway**: not every package has a Notr/Helium-style complication --
plenty are exactly as simple as the original thesis assumed. The value
of today's harder cases isn't "most packages are secretly hard," it's
"assume nothing until you've actually read the source and tried it live,"
in both directions -- some packages surprise you with hidden friction,
some just work.

### Day 1, fourth package (2026-09-09): GitGutter

Repo: jisaacks/GitGutter (2.6MB, actively maintained, well-known). 18
commands, 22 settings, real `modules/` subpackage with async task
handling.

**Result: mostly clean, one genuine "don't do that" gotcha found live,
not guessed.**

- Reading GitGutter's own diff state doesn't need a request at all --
  it's exposed as named regions (`git_gutter_inserted`, etc.) directly
  readable via `view.get_regions()`. Verified live: edited a tracked
  file's buffer (2 new lines, unsaved) and the region count updated
  correctly within ~2s -- confirms it diffs the live buffer, not the
  file on disk.
- Real mistake made and caught during testing: called
  `git_gutter_support_info` (looked like a harmless diagnostic command)
  and it hung the ST main thread -- turned out its `run()` ends in
  `sublime.message_dialog(...)`, a blocking modal. Caught via
  `diagnostics()`'s live main-thread-stack field showing the exact stuck
  call, confirmed by the user reading the dialog's actual content once
  it was dismissed. This is exactly the "do not live-invoke" class of
  command sublime-mcp's own AGENT_GUIDE.md warns about for its own UI
  commands (`prompt_goto_line`, `quick_panel`, etc.) -- GitGutter has the
  same category of trap under an innocuous-sounding name, not caught by
  introspection, only by actually calling it and watching what happened.
- Untracked-file marker rendering (`show_markers_on_untracked_file: true`)
  did not show up as expected in a quick test -- logged honestly as
  inconclusive rather than force-fit into a success or failure story.
- Skill written: ~/.claude/skills/gitgutter-control/SKILL.md, including
  the blocking-dialog warning front and center.

**Running tally after day 1 (4 packages)**: 1 clean success (OpenUri),
1 real UI-only-command workaround needed (Notr), 1 total load failure
unrelated to control technique (Helium), 1 mostly-clean-but-one-real-trap
(GitGutter). No package needed a dedicated MCP server. Every package that
loaded successfully was fully controllable via run_command/eval_python,
with specific, now-documented gotchas rather than blanket "it just
works" or "it's too complex" claims.

### Day 1, fifth package (2026-09-09): PyTest

Repo: kaste/PyTest (4.75MB, "pytest runner and view annotator"). A
genuinely professional package -- 13 commands, ships its own vendored
test suite (mockito, parameterized).

**Result: clean success via run_command, with one real scope-resolution
gotcha caught by actually running it, not by reading settings docs.**

`working_dir` defaults to `${folder}`, which resolves to the *first*
open project folder in the window -- with two broad folders open
(`~/projects` and `~/`), running from a sublime-mcp file still collected
682 tests across every project under `~/projects` and hit real,
unrelated import errors in two completely different repos. Set
`working_dir` explicitly, reran, got a clean, correctly-scoped, real
result: "collected 4 items ... 4 passed in 0.46s" matching sublime-mcp's
actual test suite exactly. No eval_python internals-reach needed at any
point -- pure run_command plus one settings fix. Reverted the setting
change afterward since it's global, not per-run. Skill written:
~/.claude/skills/pytest-control/SKILL.md.

**Takeaway**: another data point for "read the source, don't assume" --
not because the command was hard to call, but because a *default setting
value* silently did something much broader than intended. Introspection
alone (`get_package_mcp_info`) listed `working_dir` as a setting key but
gave no hint that its default was dangerous with multiple project
folders open -- only actually running it surfaced that.

### Day 1, sixth package (2026-09-09): LLM

Repo: tonylchang/sublime-llm (1.3MB, actively maintained). Real,
well-architected -- proper `sublime_llm/` subpackage with a provider
abstraction (Ollama, Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepSeek, OpenRouter, custom),
streaming, persistence, secrets handling.

**Result: complete, clean, fully-verified round trip -- the strongest
success of the night.** Already defaulted to Ollama; the machine had a
real local Ollama server running with several models pulled, so this
was the first package tonight testable against a genuinely live external
service, not just Sublime's own API. Set `model` to an actually-available
one, drove the whole flow programmatically (open chat -> insert message
into the buffer -> `sublime_llm_submit`) and got back a correct real
answer ("4" to "what is 2+2?") from the live model. No eval_python
internals-reach needed at all -- the chat view is just a plain text
buffer with `<user>`/`<assistant>` prefixes, fully driveable with the
same `view.run_command("insert", ...)` pattern used elsewhere tonight.

Real mid-test correction: the user was also typing into the same chat
view concurrently, and a read captured mid-keystroke garbled text that
looked exactly like a streaming race-condition bug at first glance.
Confirmed with the user directly rather than writing it up as a defect --
it was shared-buffer interleaving, not a plugin bug. Worth remembering:
a "bug" observed while a human is actively in the same UI needs that
ruled out before it goes in a report.

Skill written: ~/.claude/skills/llm-control/SKILL.md.

**Follow-on, same session**: continued exploring LLM interactively with
the user afterward (their idea, not scripted) -- checked `sublime_llm_show_status`
(a genuinely useful diagnostic panel, confirmed live provider
connectivity and real model lists for both Ollama and OpenAI), and along
the way hit a real, confirmed upstream bug: OpenAI's HTTP 429 covers two
different situations (`rate_limit_exceeded` vs `insufficient_quota`,
i.e. "too many requests" vs "no billing credits"), and
`providers/openai.py`'s `_map_http_error` collapses both into the same
"RATE_LIMITED... Try again shortly" message -- actively wrong advice for
the no-credits case, which the user correctly diagnosed as "no credits"
despite the plugin's own message saying otherwise. Confirmed via the
actual source (`_map_http_error`, branches purely on HTTP status, never
inspects the JSON error body), not just from the black-box symptom.
Filed: https://github.com/tonylchang/sublime-llm/issues/2

Also worth noting for method, not just result: caught myself misreading
a shared chat buffer as a "streaming race condition bug" when it was
actually the user typing concurrently -- confirmed with them before
writing it up, rather than after. Two bugs found this test (this one
real, the earlier one a near-miss caught in time) is a good illustration
of why "verify against the real thing" applies to suspected bugs just as
much as to the original thesis.

### Retroactive corrections (2026-09-09): found via the real ST console, not new tests

Reading a full console dump (triggered by the user's "you've got to be
kidding" after seeing it themselves) surfaced two things that should
have been caught earlier and weren't -- both skill files corrected:

- **LLM**: `sublime_llm_clear_chat` shows a confirmation dialog
  (`sublime.yes_no_cancel_dialog`) before clearing -- reasonable safety
  UX, not a bug. Initially mischaracterized this as a "silent failure"
  in this log; the user corrected that directly -- they saw the dialog
  and deliberately answered "No", so the chat was correctly *not*
  cleared, exactly as designed. The real, narrower finding: an agent
  cannot answer this dialog itself, so calling it programmatically hangs
  until a human responds. Corrected twice in
  ~/.claude/skills/llm-control/SKILL.md -- first to note the dialog,
  then again to fix the overstated "silent failure" framing once the
  user clarified what actually happened.
- **PyTest**: `pytest_exec.py`'s result parser throws
  `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'lxml'` on every run. The "4
  passed" result reported earlier was real (raw subprocess stdout, read
  directly), but PyTest's own richer XML-based parsing -- likely feeding
  the inline phantom annotations -- silently fails every time. Marked
  the earlier "clean success" as incomplete rather than letting it stand
  uncorrected. Corrected in ~/.claude/skills/pytest-control/SKILL.md.

**Pattern worth naming explicitly**: three unrelated packages tonight
(GitGutter, LLM, and Notr's UI-only project picker is adjacent) each had
at least one command that looks safe/informational from its name but is
actually UI-blocking or silently broken. None of this showed up from
`get_package_mcp_info`'s introspection output -- only from actually
calling things and reading the real console/traceback afterward. Also
worth naming: two of tonight's real findings (this LLM one, and the
earlier PyTest scope-resolution one) were only caught because something
was re-examined *after* an initial "it worked" conclusion, not during
the original test. Declaring success on first pass, without checking
back, would have shipped both skills with a real, silent gap.

### Day 1, seventh package (2026-09-09): R-IDE

Repo: REditorSupport/sublime-ide-r (1.5MB, actively maintained). Real,
well-structured R IDE integration. Introspection surfaced only 3 of the
real commands; reading `main.py`/`ride/buildsys/exec.py` directly found
the actual dispatch (`ride_exec_core`, callable with a raw `cmd` string
or `package`/`function`/`args`, no interactive picker required).

**Result: mechanism verified correct despite no R install on this
machine.** Didn't install R (same caution as Helium/pyzmq earlier).
Called `ride_exec_core` anyway to test the plumbing itself: it correctly
built the real subprocess invocation, resolved a working directory,
passed environment through, and failed **cleanly** via Sublime's
standard exec panel when the R binary wasn't found -- not a crash, not a
hang, a clear actionable message. Good contrast with Helium: a missing
external dependency doesn't have to mean the whole plugin fails to load:
R-IDE's design degrades gracefully at the point of actual use instead.
Skill written: ~/.claude/skills/r-ide-control/SKILL.md.

**Takeaway**: verifying "the mechanism is correct" doesn't always
require the underlying external tool to be present -- watching *how* a
package fails when a dependency is missing is itself real, useful
information, and worth doing rather than skipping the package entirely
just because full execution isn't possible.

**Takeaway for the thesis**: "no dedicated MCP needed" survives, but
"run_command args alone are always enough" does not -- some commands are
deliberately UI-only (no args accepted at all) and genuinely require the
eval_python/internals-reach fallback, not just run_command. This is a
meaningfully different, more precise claim than what was stated before
today, and it's exactly the kind of correction 3 samples wasn't enough
to surface.

**Bonus finding, unrelated to the thesis but real**: the user clicked
"Notr: Help" themselves and got a broken link. `NotrHelpCommand` hardcodes
a path assuming a loose/unzipped install (`Packages/Notr/example/
notr-spec.htm`), but Package Control installs compressed by default, so
`Packages/Notr/` doesn't exist and the command is broken for essentially
every normal user of this package. Confirmed via `os.path.isfile()`.
This is a genuine upstream bug in Notr, not a limitation of the
discover/read/call approach. Filed: https://github.com/cepthomas/Notr/issues/1

**Near-miss, corrected**: the user then tried "Open Project"/"Edit
Project" themselves and found no way to specify a project at all --
initially logged here as a second UX bug, but the package's own README
says plainly "Open a project from settings using selector" is the entire
intended workflow (hand-edit `project_files` in Package Settings,
restart). No default Context menu ships either, by design. Not a bug --
just a minimal, config-file-driven design with zero in-app onboarding
hints, which is why it read as broken. Corrected before filing a second,
wrong issue. Worth remembering: verify against the maintainer's own docs
before calling something a bug, not just against what feels intuitive.

### Day 1, ninth package (2026-09-09): AssistantAI

Repo: kanutron/AssistantAI (955KB, actively maintained). A genuinely
distinct architecture from LLM (tested earlier the same night): servers
and prompts are pure JSON data interpreted by one generic engine, not a
Python class per provider -- adding a backend means writing config, not
code.

**Result: two real findings, one structural, one a confirmed silent
failure.**

- Second instance tonight (after Markdown Images) of a legacy Python 3.3
  plugin (no `.python-version` file) -- `sys.modules` reach from
  `eval_python` is structurally impossible, confirmed empty, not a
  naming-guess failure. Only `run_command` works for this category of
  package; there is no internals-reach fallback available at all if a
  UI-only command ever needs bypassing, the way Notr's did.
- Called `assistant_ai_prompt` against real selected text two independent
  ways -- once programmatically with a guessed `pid`, once via the real
  Command Palette picker (correctly showed ~6 real prompts) with the user
  manually picking "Explain selected text" -- and got **zero visible
  feedback** both times: no console output, no dialog, no panel, no
  buffer change. Checked the one exception handler in
  `assistant_thread.py` (which does have a `print(...)` on error) -- it
  never fired, meaning the failure happens even earlier, untraced. A
  missing-credits OpenAI key (same one confirmed out of credits during
  LLM testing) is the leading suspect for *why* it failed, but the
  silence itself -- regardless of cause -- is the real, concrete gap:
  worse than R-IDE's clean error message or even Helium's load crash,
  because there's no signal at all that anything went wrong.
- Notable contrast to LLM's careful secret handling from earlier tonight:
  credentials sit directly in `.sublime-settings`, no separate secrets
  file, no env var fallback, no log redaction.
- Skill written: ~/.claude/skills/assistantai-control/SKILL.md.

**Running tally after day 1 (9 packages)**: every package that actually
loaded was controllable via run_command/eval_python (no dedicated MCP
needed anywhere), but "controllable" now has a documented range: clean
(OpenUri, LLM's core flow), needs an eval_python internals-reach
workaround (Notr), needs no request at all -- just read state (GitGutter
diffs), verified-correct-but-externally-blocked (R-IDE), and totally
inaccessible via eval_python by design (Markdown Images, AssistantAI --
legacy Python 3.3 host).

### AssistantAI follow-up (2026-09-09): silent-failure root cause fully confirmed

The user pushed back hard on leaving AssistantAI's silent failure as
"root cause not fully traced" -- correctly. They also pointed out
directly that I'd been undercrediting how much real setup burden the
package's 5-file, ~60-field configuration surface represents, having
only exercised the one field (an API key) that the shipped defaults
happened to make sufficient -- a fair correction, now folded into the
skill file.

Pushed further using the user's own real credentials file
(`C:\Users\donal\projects\secrets\api_keys.txt`, explicitly authorized
for this use) and the package's own `assistant_ai_dump` diagnostic
command (dumps the live, actually-loaded prompt/endpoint registry as
real JSON) -- confirmed config was correct all along: the OpenAI
endpoint had the real credential loaded, and the "Explain selected text"
prompt matched it with no restrictions. So the request really did fire.

Reading `assistant_ai.py`'s `handle_thread` (~line 249) found the exact,
complete answer: **every error path -- including a real OpenAI 429
insufficient-quota response -- surfaces only via
`sublime.status_message()`**, the bottom status bar text that fades in
seconds, never reaches console, and leaves no retrievable record. The
plugin worked correctly end-to-end; the entire defect is that its one
error signal lives in the UI surface most likely to be missed by a human
or an agent alike. Fully confirmed, not guessed -- both my scripted
attempt and the user's manual Command Palette click produced the
identical, now fully-explained silence. Skill file updated with the
complete root cause and the real diagnostic command
(`assistant_ai_dump`) for future use.

**Process lesson, stated plainly because it's worth remembering**: I
stopped investigating one exception handler short of the real answer
and wrote up "root cause not fully traced" as if that were an acceptable
final state. It wasn't -- the actual answer was one more file read away.
Twice tonight now (this, and the earlier LLM `sublime_llm_clear_chat`
overstatement) the user caught me settling for a plausible-sounding
account instead of the actual confirmed one. Push one level deeper before
calling an investigation done, especially when a concrete tool (like a
package's own diagnostic command) is available and unused.

## Package 10: FileBrowser (kaste/SublimeFileBrowser)

Richest command surface tested this run (50 commands). An
Emacs-dired-style file manager rendered as an editable text buffer.
Confirmed on the modern Python 3.8 plugin_host, so full `eval_python`
internals-reach applies.

Two real, confirmed findings:

1. **`assert` statements are silently no-ops in Sublime's plugin_host**
   -- it runs with `-O` (`__debug__ is False`, `sys.flags.optimize ==
   1`). `dired_create`'s `assert which in ('file', 'directory')` never
   fires; calling it with no `which` falls straight through to a
   `None.capitalize()` crash instead of a clean assertion error. This
   is a general finding about every package tested, not just this one
   -- any `assert`-based input validation in a Sublime package is not
   real validation in production.

2. **Input-panel views (from `window.show_input_panel`) are invisible
   to the normal view-discovery APIs** -- not in `window.views()`, not
   returned by `window.active_view()` (which kept returning unrelated
   views, including once the GhostShell "Claude" control tab itself),
   and not findable by scanning nearby view ids (they live in a
   separate low-id namespace, e.g. id `3`). The only reliable way found
   to get the real panel view was to monkeypatch
   `sublime.Window.show_input_panel` for one call to capture the id it
   returns, then drive that `View` directly (`insert`, then
   `dired_create_and_open`). Verified end-to-end: this created a real,
   empty file on disk at the target path, confirmed via a direct
   filesystem check afterward, not just trusting the command's `{"ok":
   true}` return.

Skill file: `~/.claude/skills/filebrowser-control/SKILL.md`. Uninstalled
after testing per the established pattern (settings entry removed,
`.sublime-package` file deleted).

**Takeaway**: this package needed the most investigative work of any
tested so far (three separate wrong assumptions before finding the real
input-panel view), but every technique that eventually worked was still
just "read the source, then use general `eval_python`/`sublime` API
tricks" -- no dedicated MCP server would have changed that discovery
cost, since the same input-panel-visibility gap exists at the raw
Sublime API level regardless of who's calling it.

10 packages fully tested and documented for day 1.

### Day 2 (2026-09-09): TreeSitter

Already installed (not a temp install for this campaign -- ships
alongside LSP/LSP-pyright/LSP-json, Debugger, and OpenUri in the user's
real config). Not a dependency of LSP despite looking like one at a
glance: checked LSP's actual `dependencies.json` (bracex, mdpopups,
orjson, typing_extensions, wcmatch) and grepped its source for any
`tree_sitter` reference -- none. They're independent packages that
happen to both be installed; LSP gets code understanding from a real
language-server process over stdio, no parser library involved.

14 commands total (`Default.sublime-commands`), all structural
selection/navigation/debugging on top of a live Tree-sitter parse tree
maintained per-buffer in `TreeSitter.src.core.BUFFER_ID_TO_TREE`.
Verified live against `sublime_mcp.py` itself (6196 lines):

- `tree_sitter_print_tree` -- opens a debug view rendering the syntax
  tree (or subtree under selection). Confirmed real: the debug view
  survived a full Sublime Text restart via session-restore, proving it
  wrote a real view, not just returned `{"ok": true}`.
- `tree_sitter_select_ancestor` -- expanded a cursor placed inside the
  module docstring to select the entire docstring node (~2400 chars),
  confirmed by reading the live selection via `eval_python` afterward
  rather than trusting the command's return value.
- `tree_sitter_select_symbols` -- ran the bundled `python/symbols.scm`
  Tree-sitter query against the whole buffer and selected 380 real
  symbol regions (module-level assignments, every `def`, etc.),
  confirmed by reading back the selected lines.

No dedicated MCP server needed -- get_package_mcp_info's discover ->
read source (`src/api.py`, `src/core.py`) -> call via `run_command`
loop was sufficient, same as every other package tested.

**Real, unrelated bug found via this testing, not a TreeSitter issue**:
sublime-mcp's own `run_command`/`get_view_content` `name=` tab-targeting
silently failed to match `sublime_mcp.py` by filename (matched only
`view.name()`, empty for any normal saved file) -- caught because a
TreeSitter command needed to target a specific tab by name while the
Claude control tab held global focus. Fixed and released as
**sublime-mcp 1.7.4** (PyPI, npm, MCP Registry, GitHub `main`) same
session. See `project_gadzillion_package_test_campaign` memory for the
full writeup -- this is a good example of the campaign's own
methodology (use a package for real, don't just audit sublime-mcp)
surfacing a real defect that a code review might have missed.

Also hit, and worth remembering for future sessions: editing
`sublime_mcp.py` live on disk while it was actively serving the MCP
request that triggered its own plugin reload wedged the plugin_host
main thread (every call, even `get_help`, hung for 300s and had to be

Author `kaste`/`timbrel`. By far the largest command surface tested in

list). A full git+GitHub/GitLab UI inside Sublime -- status dashboard,
inline diff staging, interactive rebase, log graph, bisect, git-flow,
blame, line history, PR/MR review.

Verified live against the real `sublime-mcp` repo:

- `gs_show_status` -- opened a real "STATUS: sublime-mcp" dashboard
  view. Confirmed accurate, not just rendered: showed the correct
  branch (`main` tracking `origin/main`), the correct HEAD commit
  (`7739ac2`, matching the 1.7.4 release commit made earlier this
  session), and the correct untracked files (`.claude/`,
  `.package_skill_test_log.md`) -- cross-checked against `git status`
  independently.
- `gs_log_current_branch` -- opened an interactive quick panel (commit

  details for the highlighted commit. Confirms the sublime-mcp
  AGENT_GUIDE's own warning ("Do not... live-invoke quick_panel tools")
  is correct for this package: quick-panel-based commands aren't
  capturable as a static view the way `gs_show_status`'s dashboard is.

**Real gotcha found, another blocking-modal-dialog trap** (same
category as GitGutter's `support_info` and LLM's `clear_chat` found
earlier in this campaign): `gs_show_status` determines "is this window
a git repo" from the **active view's file path**, not the window's
project folders. Called once while the no-path "Claude" control tab
had global focus, GitSavvy's `core/commands/init.py` decided the
window wasn't a git repo and tried to show a blocking native
`sublime.ok_cancel_dialog` ("no repository found, initialize one?"),
which hung the plugin_host main thread for 5+ seconds (every other
sublime-mcp call, e.g. `get_open_files`, timed out during that window)
before it cleared on its own without any explicit dismiss action taken.
Retried successfully after first `eval_python`-focusing a real
in-repo file view (`sublime_mcp.py`) -- confirms the fix is always
ensure a real file view has focus before invoking any GitSavvy
WindowCommand, not just having the right window/project active.

No dedicated MCP server needed -- same discover/read-source/call loop
worked even at this scale; the only real friction was the focus-
dependent repo-detection gotcha above, which is a live-Sublime-API
quirk (native modal dialogs), not something a dedicated MCP server
would sidestep either.

### Day 2 (2026-09-09): Terminus

Author `randy3k`. ~32 commands, real PTY-backed terminal emulator
inside Sublime -- this is the package GhostShell's own `ai_terminal`

what the competing/predecessor implementation actually does.

Verified live, real subprocess round-trip:

  output panel backed by an actual spawned shell (`cmd.exe` on

  `{"ok": true}`.

  the PTY; the marker string round-tripped back into the panel's
  buffer, confirming a real, working PTY write/read cycle end to end.

not a bug)**: Terminus panels are Sublime *output panels*

addressable tabs the same way -- had to fall back to `eval_python` +
`window.find_output_panel(name)` directly. This is a real gap for
anyone wanting to script Terminus (or any output-panel-based package)
via sublime-mcp, worth a future enhancement (a `get_panel_content`-
style tool) rather than a bug in the 1.7.4 fix.

buffer content before and after rather than trusting `{"ok": true}`:

CSS abbreviation typed at the top level of a `.css` file (outside any

(not just cursor position) drives whether a live-invoked text command

from the following line and correctly inferred `callback` specifically

### Day 2 (2026-09-09): ColorPicker

`Weslly H.`, #4-ish by installs among CSS-adjacent tooling. Picked
specifically to test an axis nothing else in the campaign had hit yet:
a package whose real action is a **native OS modal dialog**, not a
Sublime quick panel or input panel.

**New failure mode, confirmed by source**: on Windows, the actual color
picker is `ctypes.windll.Comdlg32.ChooseColorW` -- a real Win32 common
dialog, called directly via `ctypes` with a `CHOOSECOLOR` struct
(`sublimecp.py`). This is categorically different from every earlier
blocking-dialog trap in this campaign (GitGutter/LLM/GitSavvy's
`sublime.ok_cancel_dialog`, FileBrowser/BracketHighlighter's
`show_quick_panel`): those are Sublime-level and *can* be driven --
pre-focus the right view to dodge them, or monkeypatch
`sublime.ok_cancel_dialog`/`show_quick_panel` to capture the callback
and drive it programmatically. `ChooseColorW` is a real OS-level modal
owned by the Win32 message loop, with no Python-reachable hook at all
-- there's no callback to monkeypatch, no `on_select` to intercept. A
scripted caller can start it but cannot finish it headlessly; it can
only be closed by a real UI actor (a human, or a UI-automation tool
that manipulates the native dialog's window handle -- outside anything
`eval_python`/`run_command` reaches).

Deliberately did not invoke the real command to confirm this live --
doing so would pop a real modal and require manual dismissal to un-wedge
the window, for a fact the source already establishes unambiguously.
Documented as a genuine, expected boundary of the "no dedicated MCP
needed" thesis: it was never about replacing OS-native UI, only about
Sublime's own package layer. A `computer-use`-style tool that can drive
native dialogs by window handle would be the only way past this one --
not a sublime-mcp gap.

No dedicated MCP server needed for anything sublime-mcp could reach
(same as always) -- the boundary here is the OS, not the package.
Uninstalled after testing (`remove_package`).

### Correction (2026-09-09): `remove_package` was never actually removing anything

Caught this resuming the session: both "Uninstalled after testing
(`remove_package`)" claims above (SideBarEnhancements, ColorPicker) were
**false**. `run_command("remove_package", {"package": name})` returned
`{"ok": true}` from sublime-mcp's wrapper, but the real ST console
showed `TypeError: run() got an unexpected keyword argument 'package'`
both times -- `ok: true` just means the command dispatched without the
*wrapper* raising, not that the underlying ST command succeeded.
Package Control's `remove_package` `WindowCommand.run()` takes **no
package-name argument at all** -- reading
`package_control.commands.remove_package_command` showed it's a pure
quick-panel picker (`ExistingPackagesCommand` base): it always pops a
panel of installed packages and only calls `on_done(manager,
package_name)` after a live UI selection. There is no scriptable arg
path through the command layer at all -- not a wrong-arg-name problem,
a wrong-command problem. Confirmed both packages were still genuinely
installed via `manager.list_packages()` directly.

Fixed by going straight to Package Control's internals (the same
discover/read-source/call-directly loop this whole campaign is built
on, just applied to the removal side for once): instantiate
`PackageManager()` and `PackageTaskRunner(manager)` from
`Package Control.package_control.package_manager`/`package_tasks`
directly via `eval_python`, then
`PackageTaskRunner(manager).remove_packages({names}, progress)` inside
an `ActivityIndicator()` context -- removes cleanly, verified via
`list_packages()` before/after, no UI interaction needed.

**Standing methodology fix for the rest of this campaign**: a
`run_command` result of `ok: true` only proves sublime-mcp's dispatcher
didn't except -- it does *not* prove the underlying ST command
succeeded. From here, cross-check any consequential `run_command` call
(especially ones with no return value to inspect) against the real
console output before trusting it. Not fixing older log entries
retroactively (not worth the churn), but future entries state
`remove_packages` (internals-reach, verified) explicitly rather than
`remove_package`.

### Day 2 (2026-09-09): WakaTime

`wakatime` org, real time-tracking/analytics plugin -- picked to test
two axes nothing earlier in the campaign combined: a package that
manages its own external compiled binary (downloads `wakatime-cli` from
GitHub releases into `Packages/WakaTime/wakatime-cli/` on first load,
completely separate from the Package Control zip) and whose real
"do something" path is entirely event-driven (`on_post_save`/
`on_modified`/`on_selection_modified`), not a single ST command at all
-- the only registered command, `wakatime_dashboard`, just opens a
browser tab.

**New trap found**: `plugin_loaded()` -> `after_loaded()` ->
`prompt_api_key()` silently opens a real `show_input_panel` for the
WakaTime API key immediately on load if none is configured, with no
console message beyond the panel's own "Enter your WakaTime API key:"
prompt -- `window.active_panel()` confirmed `"input"` was open,
unnoticed, with nothing else pending. Same trap family as Notr's
UI-only prompts, but a new variant: this one fires automatically on
package *load*, not on a command -- simply installing the package (no
command invocation at all) leaves an unclosed input panel sitting over
the window. `run_command("hide_panel")` closed it cleanly.

**Real methodology finding, sys.modules gap**: unlike every other
package tested in this campaign, `WakaTime.WakaTime` never appeared in
`sys.modules` under any lookup (exact key, substring, prefix) despite
the console clearly logging `reloading python 3.3 plugin
WakaTime.WakaTime` with no error. Root cause not chased down (spent the
time budget on the trap above instead) -- worked around it by loading
the file fresh via `importlib.util.spec_from_file_location` directly
against the real path on disk rather than relying on the ST module
registry, then called `handle_activity(view, is_write=True)` on a real
saved file straight from that fresh module object. Confirmed the whole
pipeline runs end to end without any ST command: `HEARTBEATS.qsize()`
went from 0 to 1, i.e. a real heartbeat was queued exactly like a real
save would produce. Worth remembering as a fallback pattern if
`sys.modules` lookup ever comes up empty for a package that's
definitely loaded: `importlib.util.spec_from_file_location` against the
known `python_files` path is a working escape hatch.

No dedicated MCP server needed. Uninstalled after testing via the fixed
`PackageTaskRunner.remove_packages` internals-reach method, verified
against `list_packages()`.

20 packages fully tested and documented, day 2.

### Day 2 (2026-09-09): RemoteSubl -- deliberately picked to attack the thesis, not just sample it

`randy3k`'s active fork of `henrikpersson/rsub` (the rmate protocol for
Sublime). Picked specifically because its architecture is the inverse of
every package tested so far: `plugin_loaded()` starts a raw
`socketserver.ThreadingTCPServer` on `localhost:52698` and *waits for an
external client to connect* (the real `rmate`/`mate` shell script,
normally piped in over an SSH `-R` tunnel from a remote box). Every
other package in this campaign exposes behavior the agent calls *into*
via `run_command`/`eval_python`; this one exposes nothing callable at
all -- `get_package_mcp_info` surfaced exactly one command
(`edit_settings`, boilerplate). If any package was going to need a real
standing MCP server acting as an external client, this looked like the
one.

**Result: thesis holds even here, but the first pass overstated it --
caught and corrected before closing this entry, same discipline as the
LLM/AssistantAI corrections above.** `eval_python` is not limited to
Sublime's own API -- it's a full embedded Python interpreter, so it can
just `import socket` and *be* the external rmate client itself, in the
same process, no separate process or server required.

- Opened a raw `socket.create_connection(('localhost', 52698))`,
  received the real banner (`Sublime Text 3 (remote_subl plugin)`).
- Sent a real `open` / `display-name` / `real-path` / `token` / `data: N`
  frame per the rmate wire protocol (reverse-engineered directly from
  `remote_subl.py`'s `Session.parse_input`, not from external docs).
- Confirmed a real file materialized with the exact sent content, read
  back via `view.substr()` on the actual opened view.

Initially logged this as a "full real protocol round trip," which was
wrong: that first test only exercised the inbound half (client -> open
file). The socket lived in one `eval_python` call's locals, which don't
survive to the next call, so it was already dead by the time the file's
view was closed -- confirmed directly in the ST console:
`New connection ... 21:44:41` / `Connection ... is closed. 21:44:54`
(closed on its own, ~13s later, when the dead socket was garbage
collected) / `Error closing rmate_test.txt in testhost. 21:45:00` (the
`on_close` handler's `file.close()` tried `session.send("close")` on
the already-closed socket, raised, and skipped its own `os.unlink`/
`os.rmdir` -- confirmed the temp file and directory were still on disk
afterward, cleaned up manually). No `CONNECTION_LOST` dialog text
appeared in the console for the natural disconnect, and every
subsequent call kept responding promptly, so the background handler
thread's `cleanup()` (which does call a real `sublime.message_dialog`
on disconnect by default) did not visibly wedge the main thread here --
but the earlier claim of a clean full round trip was still not earned.

Went back and settled the actual crux directly, since it generalizes
past this one package: **can `eval_python` hold a live socket open
across separate calls at all**, the way a real rmate session (or any
other TCP-backed control scheme) needs to stay open for the life of an
edit session? Confirmed yes, with a generic test unrelated to
RemoteSubl -- stashed a live loopback socket pair as an attribute on
the already-imported `sublime` module (a persistent object across calls
in the same long-lived plugin_host process) in one `eval_python` call,
then sent/received real bytes both directions from a second, separate
call. This is the actual mechanism that would make a genuine rmate
save-back round trip (or a hypothetical write-your-own-rmate-client
MCP tool) work via plain `eval_python` -- confirmed generically rather
than assumed from the narrower, already-corrected RemoteSubl test.

No dedicated MCP server needed. Uninstalled after testing via the
`PackageTaskRunner.remove_packages` internals-reach method, verified
against `list_packages()` and against nothing still listening on 52698.

**Takeaway, and the actual point of this entry**: "genuinely needs a
dedicated MCP" would require a client protocol `eval_python` truly
cannot speak -- not just an unusual *direction* of control, and not
just a connection that has to outlive a single tool call (confirmed
separately that it can, via the persistent-module-attribute pattern).
A listen-and-wait TCP server is not that: `eval_python`'s Python
interpreter can dial in as the client, and hold the connection open
across calls, just as easily as it can call a Sublime command. The
remaining candidates that could actually force a dedicated MCP are
narrower than "runs its own server" -- e.g. a native OS-modal dialog
with no scriptable handle (ColorPicker's `ChooseColorW`, already found
and documented above) or a binary/proprietary wire format `eval_python`
has no library for. Both would need testing on their own merits, not
inferred from "it manages a server."

21 packages fully tested and documented, day 2.

### Day 2 (2026-09-09): LiveReload -- testing the remaining "binary/proprietary wire format" candidate named above

`alepez`'s LiveReload-sublimetext3 fork. Picked as the direct follow-on to
RemoteSubl's takeaway: a package whose real protocol is a hand-rolled
RFC6455 WebSocket implementation (`server/WebSocketClient.py`,
`WebSocketServer.py`) -- real HTTP-Upgrade handshake with a SHA1/base64
`Sec-WebSocket-Accept` computation, then binary HyBi framing (FIN/opcode
byte, extended-length markers, client-side XOR masking) -- with no
external websocket library involved on either side, the closest thing in
this corpus to the "binary/proprietary wire format `eval_python` has no
library for" case.

**Result: thesis holds for the protocol itself, fully verified; the
push-notification half was left unconfirmed after my own tooling mistake
disrupted the session, documented honestly rather than papered over.**

- Full real WebSocket handshake done from `eval_python` using only
  `socket`/`hashlib`/`base64`/`struct` (all embedded-Python stdlib, no
  `websockets` package): computed a real `Sec-WebSocket-Key`, sent the
  HTTP Upgrade request, and independently recomputed the expected
  `Sec-WebSocket-Accept` value to verify the server's response matched
  the real RFC6455 formula rather than just checking for `101`.
- Sent a real masked HyBi text frame (`{"command":"hello",...}`) and
  received back the server's real, correctly-parsed unmasked frame
  (`0x81 0x7e <2-byte length> <json>`) containing the actual protocol
  list LiveReload's `onreceive()` sends on successful hello. Full,
  correct client-to-server AND server-to-client binary framing verified
  both directions -- not just "connected," a real bidirectional protocol
  round trip.
- `sys.modules` lookups for `LiveReload` came back completely empty from
  the `eval_python` host (confirmed `sys.version` there is 3.8.12) even
  though the server was clearly running -- confirmed via source
  (`CommandAPI.py` successfully does `import LiveReload` in its own file)
  that this package loads on the **legacy Python 3.3 plugin host**, a
  genuinely separate OS process from the one `eval_python` reaches, not
  just a separate module namespace. Sockets are OS-level and reachable
  regardless of which host owns the listener, which is exactly why the
  protocol-level test above still worked -- but this is the first
  package in the campaign where the internals-reach fallback (`sys.modules`,
  monkeypatching `show_quick_panel`) is **structurally**, not just
  practically, unavailable, because it would require code execution
  inside a different OS process entirely.
- Found the actual push trigger (`SimpleReloadPlugin.py`'s `on_post_save`)
  is gated by `enabled_plugins` (default `[]` -- disabled out of the box,
  same settings-default-trap pattern as PyTest's `working_dir` and
  WakaTime's auto-prompt), and that the normal UI path to toggle it
  (`LiveReloadEnablePluginCommand`) is quick-panel-only with zero args --
  another case that would need the now-unavailable-here monkeypatch
  fallback. Worked around it the settings-file way instead (write
  `enabled_plugins` to `Packages/User/LiveReload.sublime-settings` *before*
  the plugin (re)loads, since its `PluginFactory` metaclass captures
  `enabled_plugins` once from `Settings()` at class-definition time and
  never re-reads it later) -- confirmed this is a general, available
  technique distinct from the blocked internals-reach one.
- Attempting to trigger the actual save that would exercise the
  push-back half is where this entry stops short: repeated
  `run_command("save", scope="window", name=...)` calls did not target
  the intended file at all -- `name`/`index` targeting only applies for
  `scope="view"/"text"` per the tool's own schema, so `scope="window"`
  silently saved whatever view was globally focused instead, and at
  least once that was an untitled/unsaved view, which popped Sublime's
  native "Save As" dialog and blocked the window. Every "5s main-thread
  timeout" symptom I saw was this dialog, not a LiveReload hang or
  system contention as first guessed -- the user had to notice and
  reject it directly, twice, before it was correctly diagnosed. Recorded
  as its own gotcha, independent of this package: see
  `sublime_mcp_run_command_window_scope_name_gotcha` /
  `feedback_screenshot_verify_before_after` in the assistant's memory.
  Did not re-attempt the live push-confirmation after that -- stopped
  testing for the session once real UI was popping in front of the user.

No dedicated MCP server needed for anything actually tested (the full
bidirectional WS protocol, confirmed request/response both ways). The
push-trigger's live confirmation is an honest gap, not a thesis failure
-- it was blocked by my own mis-targeted `run_command` call, not by
anything about LiveReload or the protocol. Uninstalled after testing via
`PackageTaskRunner.remove_packages`, verified against `list_packages()`.

**Takeaway**: the "binary/proprietary wire format" candidate named in
the RemoteSubl entry's takeaway turned out to be handleable the same way
as everything else -- `eval_python`'s stdlib (`socket`, `hashlib`,
`base64`, `struct`) is enough to speak a hand-rolled binary protocol
correctly, including verifying the cryptographic handshake step by
independent recomputation rather than trusting a status code. The
genuinely new, real finding here is different from what was being
searched for: **the legacy Python 3.3 plugin host is a separate OS
process, not just a separate namespace** -- for packages hosted there,
`eval_python`'s internals-reach escape hatch (which saved Notr,
FileBrowser, BracketHighlighter, and others) is categorically
unavailable, not merely untried. `run_command` args still work fine
across hosts (ST's core command router handles that transparently), so
a legacy-hosted package is only actually blocked when it *also* has a
UI-only command with no args and no alternate settings-based path --
LiveReload had exactly one such command, but a settings-file workaround
existed anyway. A legacy-hosted package that combined "quick-panel-only
required action" with "no settings-file escape hatch" would be the
sharper version of this test, not yet found.

22 packages fully tested and documented, day 2.

### Day 2 (2026-09-09): AdvancedNewFile -- the sharper test found, and this time the thesis needed a real fix, not a workaround

`SublimeText`'s AdvancedNewFile (last touched 2015 -- a decade stale,
confirmed legacy Python 3.3 host via empty `sys.modules` lookups from the
`eval_python` py3.8 host, same signature as LiveReload/AssistantAI/
Markdown Images). Picked specifically as the sharper version of
LiveReload's unresolved takeaway: a legacy-hosted package whose core
action (`advanced_new_file_new`) is entirely input-panel-driven with zero
scriptable args for the part that matters (`initial_path` only pre-fills
text; the file is only actually created via the panel's `on_done`), and
with no settings-file escape hatch this time (unlike LiveReload's
`enabled_plugins`).

**Result: this is the one case in 23 packages where "read source, then
call directly" genuinely could not finish the job on its own -- and it
led to fixing sublime-mcp itself instead of just documenting a gap.**

- Confirmed the FileBrowser-era monkeypatch trick (patch
  `sublime.Window.show_input_panel` from `eval_python` to capture the
  real `on_done` callback) cannot apply here at all: that patch lives in
  the py3.8 host's own `sublime` module object, a different OS process
  entirely from the py3.3 host that actually calls `show_input_panel`.
  Not "harder," structurally impossible -- confirmed, not assumed.
- Tested whether `view.run_command("insert", {"characters": "\n"})` on
  the input panel's view (found via the established low-id
  `sublime.View(id)` scan + `is_widget`/window match) could simulate
  Enter, the way it sometimes can for other kinds of text widgets. It
  cannot: the character is silently accepted into the buffer (confirmed
  visually via screenshot) but never submits -- Sublime's input-panel
  submission is a native keybinding, not something the `insert` command
  triggers.
- Read Sublime's own `Default (Windows).sublime-keymap` resource directly
  (not guessed, not from external docs) and found the real bindings:
  Enter in an input panel is `{"command": "select", "context":
  [{"panel_has_focus": true}, {"panel_type": "input"}]}`; Escape is
  `{"command": "hide_panel", "args": {"cancel": true}, "context":
  [{"panel_visible": true}]}`. Both `select` and `hide_panel` are built-in
  ST commands implemented in the native binary, not Python -- calling
  them via `window.run_command` reaches the panel's real `on_done`/
  `on_cancel` callback correctly *regardless of which plugin_host process
  registered it*, since ST's own core command router (not `eval_python`)
  does the cross-process dispatch. Verified live: `w.run_command("select")`
  on a filled-in panel created a real file at the given path and opened
  it exactly like a real user submitting the prompt would; a second run
  with `action="cancel"` correctly did not create its file.
- **This is a real, confirmed exception to "no dedicated MCP server
  needed" as originally scoped** -- not because a *standing* MCP server
  was the fix, but because `eval_python`/`run_command` as sublime-mcp
  shipped them that morning genuinely could not drive this command
  end-to-end (no reachable view, no working submit path). Rather than
  leave it as a documented gap or reach for a per-package dedicated MCP,
  fixed it at the right layer: added a new **generic** sublime-mcp tool,
  `drive_input_panel` (fills and submits/cancels *any* open input panel,
  not just AdvancedNewFile's), released as sublime-mcp 1.7.6. Full
  writeup: `sublime_mcp_drive_input_panel_tool` in the assistant's memory.
  This keeps the campaign's actual thesis intact at the tool level
  ("sublime-mcp is enough, don't build per-package MCP servers") while
  being honest that the *specific two verbs* (`run_command`, `eval_python`)
  named at the campaign's start were not, by themselves, sufficient for
  every package -- a third, now-generic verb was needed and got added.
- **Real incident during this fix, not part of the package finding
  itself:** editing `sublime_mcp.py` live (once to add the tool, again to
  bump `__version__`) reproduced the self-reload hang from
  `sublime_mcp_self_edit_bricked_st` twice in a row -- every sublime-mcp
  call including `diagnostics` hung and got moved to background tasks.
  Both times, a plain external `taskkill <pid>` + relaunch
  `sublime_text.exe` recovered fully in under 10 seconds, with the
  project, tabs, and the live ai_terminal/Claude session surviving via
  existing session-restore + `agent_broker.py` persistence -- much
  milder than the original 2026-09-06 incident's "no recovery of any
  kind." Also made real mistakes worth naming plainly: repeated
  `run_command("save", scope="window", name=...)` calls on the previous
  (LiveReload) package popped a real "Save As" dialog the user had to
  reject twice before it was correctly diagnosed (scope="window" ignores
  `name`/`index` targeting entirely -- see
  `sublime_mcp_run_command_window_scope_name_gotcha`), and this session
  let two separate hung sublime-mcp calls sit for their full 2-minute
  background-task timeout before acting, which the user correctly called
  out as too slow -- a screenshot or `diagnostics()` gives the same
  signal in seconds.

Uninstalled AdvancedNewFile after testing via the established
`PackageTaskRunner.remove_packages` method, verified against
`list_packages()`.

**Takeaway**: 23 packages in, the campaign found its first genuine,
confirmed case where sublime-mcp's existing tools weren't enough on their
own -- and the right response was a small, generic addition to
sublime-mcp itself (reusable by any future package with the same shape),
not a per-package dedicated MCP server and not settling for "this one
can't be fully driven." The original thesis survives in its strongest,
most useful form: *some* general-purpose tool in sublime-mcp is always
enough, even if that tool doesn't exist yet at the moment a package is
first tested.

23 packages fully tested and documented, day 2.

### Correction (2026-09-14): test criterion sharpened, no installs occurred

The user corrected the framing of the Day 3 batch above after the fact.
Two things to set straight:

1. **No package was installed live this session, for any candidate,
   under any framing.** There was no live Sublime MCP connection
   available in this session at all -- every Day 3 verdict was already
   source-read triage only, as stated at the top of that entry. Nothing
   to uninstall.
2. **The real test is narrower than "does it use an already-confirmed-safe
   category."** Correct question, applied per package: find the single
   most native/hardware/OS-dependent operation the package's source
   actually performs, then ask only whether that specific operation has
   a Python-side hook -- something `eval_python` running in the same
   process could call, read, or block on -- versus a raw OS call
   (ctypes Win32 dialog, COM object, kernel handle) that blocks with
   *no* accessible callback once invoked. ColorPicker's
   `ctypes.windll.Comdlg32.ChooseColorW` is the one confirmed instance
   of the latter. `subprocess.Popen`, `socket.socket`, `threading.Thread`,
   `mmap`, `os.pipe`, and any `sublime.*`/`sublime_plugin.*` API call all
   have a Python-side handle by construction -- the process invoking them
   is the same Python process eval_python runs in -- so those were never
   actually "pattern-matched," they satisfy the narrow test directly.

Re-checked each Day 3 "no" verdict against the narrow question
specifically (not re-installed, not re-read from scratch -- re-derived
from the same source citations already gathered): every one names a
`subprocess`/`socket`/`threading`/`mmap`/plain-Sublime-API call as its
most native operation, and every one of those has a live Python object
(a `Popen`, a `socket`, a `Thread`, a `View`) reachable from the same
process -- so all 17 "no" verdicts and the CMake N/A stand unchanged
under the corrected test. ColorHelper's "yes" stands unchanged: its
native path is a direct `ctypes` call into `Comdlg32.ChooseColorW`,
which blocks in an OS-owned modal loop with no Python frame on the
stack until the user closes it -- no hook, full stop.
