rather than trusted from the orchestrator's own summary. See
[[feedback_never_override_given_selection_criteria]] -- the fan-out is
the same failure pattern (inventing scale/method that was never asked
for) applied to a delegated agent instead of this session directly.


### 2026-09-14 (later, same day): whole-corpus pass, written in plain English

The user asked to get through the entire Package Control catalog today,
not keep hand-picking one package at a time -- and to write this pass up
in plain English a non-programmer could follow, not technical shorthand.
(A first version of this same pass was written in dense jargon and was
discarded and redone as the text below, at the user's request.)

**How the list was narrowed down first.** Package Control publicly lists,
for every package it distributes, how many people have ever installed it
and when it was last updated. Every single package in the catalog was
pulled down (5,425 of them once duplicates are removed) along with those
two numbers. Then two simple rules were applied by a script, not by
looking at each one by hand: a package only made the shortlist if (1) it
has been installed at least 10,000 times ever (a real, solid amount of
use, not just a few downloads) and (2) it has been updated sometime in
the last two years (so it isn't an abandoned relic). 63 packages already
looked at earlier in this campaign were set aside and not re-checked.
That left 5,362 packages to test against the two rules. **5,179 of them
failed one or both rules and were dropped as one batch, without looking
at any of them individually** -- some were recently updated but not
popular enough, some were popular but hadn't been touched in years, and
most failed both. The "last updated" date from Package Control was spot
checked against each surviving package's real GitHub history to make
sure it wasn't misleading, and it matched every time. One extra package,
a color theme called "Theme - El Capitan," looked recent by that date but
turned out to have been formally archived (retired) by its own author on
GitHub, so it was dropped too. That left **182 packages** that are both
genuinely popular and still actively maintained -- the real shortlist.

**What was checked for each of the 182.** For every one of them, the
actual source code was downloaded from its GitHub repository and read.
Two things were being looked for. First, a basic compatibility check:
does the package actually support the current version of Sublime Text's
scripting engine, or is it stuck supporting only the old, long-obsolete
one? (Package Control's "last updated" date can be misleading here --
a package can get a fresh update that only touches its documentation or
color scheme, without ever being upgraded to work with the current
engine.) Second, and this is the real question the whole campaign is
about: when the package does its main job, does it ever hand control
over to something that Sublime Text's scripting layer can no longer see
or touch once it starts -- the clearest real-world example found so far
being a package that pops open your operating system's own native
color-picker window. Once that window is open, it is a separate program
with its own controls; nothing running inside Sublime Text can read it,
click its buttons, or close it, until a human does that by hand. That is
the one kind of thing that would genuinely require building a separate,
dedicated tool just for that package. Everything else -- running another
program and reading its output, opening a network connection, showing a
menu or a text prompt inside Sublime Text itself, doing work in the
background -- is something that can always be watched and driven from
the outside, because it all still happens inside processes and objects
that Sublime Text's own scripting layer has a live handle on.

**Results of that check:**

- **46 of the 182 turned out not to be real plugins at all** -- they are
  just visual add-ons (a color theme, an icon set, a syntax-highlighting
  definition, a snippet pack) with no actual running program inside them.
  There is nothing to "control" in these at all, the same way there was
  nothing to control in a build-system package looked at earlier in the
  campaign. (Full list: ApacheConf, Brackets Color Scheme, C++ & C Single
  File Builder - Minghang Yang, Catppuccin color schemes, Cisco, Decent
  Swift Syntax, DoxyDoxygen, Dracula Color Scheme, Enhanced HTML and CFML,
  FileIcons, FileIcons Mono, Generic Config, GitHub Theme, Github Color
  Theme, Handlebars, JQ Syntax, Kotlin, Mermaid, Neon Color Scheme, Nim,
  Notepad++ Color Scheme, Nunjucks, PowerShell, React + Js Snippets,
  Smarty, Solarized Color Scheme, Svelte, TOML, Tailwind CSS, Terraform,
  Theme - Brackets, Theme - Monokai Pro, Theme - One, Theme - Spacegray,
  VimL, Visual Studio Code Plus Scheme, XAML, x86 and x86_64 Assembly,
  zenburn, EJS, Jinja2, Laravel Blade, Liquid, PostCSS, Twig, Vue.)

- **39 of the 182 were dropped because they never actually upgraded to
  work with Sublime Text's current scripting engine**, even though
  Package Control shows them as "recently updated." Reading their code
  confirmed they are still written for the old engine that was retired
  years ago -- the recent update was something cosmetic, like a
  documentation tweak, not a real code migration. Per the rule this
  campaign has followed the whole time, these were not investigated any
  further than that one check. (Full list: Auto Close HTML Tags, CSS3,
  Calculate, ChangeQuotes, Clipboard Manager, Color Highlight, Comments
  Aware Enter, CoolFormat, CursorRuler, DictionaryAutoComplete,
  ESLint-Formatter, Elixir, Emacs Pro Essentials, GitHubinator, Gitignore,
  Guna, HTML (C#), JsPrettier, LanguageTool, LocalizedMenu, NASM x86
  Assembly, Ngx HTML, PlantUmlDiagrams, Prettierd Format, Restructured
  Text (RST) Snippets, SQF Language, SystemVerilog, Table Editor,
  TextFormatting, TodoTxt Syntax, Translator, Transparency,
  UIkitCompletions, UnicodeConverter, Unity Shader, Verilog Gadget, fish,
  wpseek WordPress Developer Assistant, xml2json.

- **The remaining 97 packages were real, running plugins, and every
  single one of them turned out to be something the AI can already fully
  operate without any special extra tool.** None of them pop open one of
  those un-drivable native OS windows. Here is what each one actually
  does and why it's fine, in plain terms:

  - **38 of the 97 are small helper packages for a linting framework
    called SublimeLinter** (one for JSHint, one for PHP's linter, one for
    ESLint, and so on -- the full list is: jshint, php, csslint, eslint,
    html-tidy, phplint, pylint, phpcs, pep8, jsxhint, pyflakes, clang,
    xmllint, ruby, pug-lint, rubocop, jsl, javac, cppcheck, pycodestyle,
    jscs, shellcheck, tslint, bandit, cpplint, coffee, phpmd, lua,
    stylelint, gjslint, coffeelint, pydocstyle, pyyaml, chktex, flow,
    luacheck, golint, and one for a custom syntax-checking format). Every
    single one of these is just a tiny settings file telling the main
    SublimeLinter program which external checking tool to run and how to
    read its output -- they don't do anything themselves beyond that, and
    the main SublimeLinter program itself was already fully checked
    earlier in this campaign and found to be completely controllable.

  - **16 of the 97 are similar small helper packages, but for a
    different framework called LSP**, which connects Sublime Text to
    various programming-language "smart assistant" tools (one each for
    TypeScript, JSON, the Clangd C/C++ tool, GitHub Copilot, Python,
    PHP's Intelephense tool, Rust, HTML, Go's Gopls tool, CSS, ESLint,
    YAML, Dockerfiles, a file-watching helper, Vue, and Bash). Like the
    linter helpers above, these are thin configuration wrappers around
    the main LSP program, which was already checked earlier in the
    campaign and found fully controllable. The biggest one of the sixteen,
    the GitHub Copilot helper, was read in full since it's unusually
    large -- it just talks to GitHub's servers over a normal web
    connection and shows suggestions inside Sublime Text; nothing native
    or hidden in it either.

  - **Package Control itself** -- the program that installs and removes
    all these other packages -- was checked too, since it's popular
    enough to qualify. It runs other programs, downloads files over the
    internet, and does background work, all of which is normal and fully
    watchable. It does call two very small pieces of Windows' own
    plumbing directly (checking a file's read-only/hidden flags, and
    clearing an internal Windows error flag), but those are simple,
    instant lookups that hand control straight back to the program --
    nothing like a window popping open and waiting for a human.

  - **Sass** just reads what you're typing and offers autocomplete
    suggestions for Sass stylesheets. No outside programs, no windows,
    nothing to intercept.

  - **A File Icon** changes the little file-type icons shown in the
    sidebar by writing out a theme file based on your settings. Purely
    internal file writing, no popups.

  - **MarkdownEditing** adds nice editing behavior for Markdown files. It
    can hand text off to an external formatting program and can check a
    link over the internet, both of which are ordinary background work
    Sublime Text can watch happen and get the result from.

  - **Indent XML** just reformats XML/JSON text neatly. It's a pure
    text-in, text-out operation on the file you're editing.

  - **CoffeeScript** support compiles CoffeeScript files by handing the
    text to the real `coffee` command-line compiler and showing you the
    result, sometimes doing that on a background thread so Sublime Text
    doesn't freeze while it waits. That's an ordinary, watchable
    background job.

  - **EditorConfig** reads project style settings (like tab width) from a
    config file and quietly applies them when you open or save a file.
    No windows, no external programs.

  - **PlainTasks** is a to-do-list manager that lives entirely inside a
    normal text file, with menus and background checking for you to pick
    from. Fully normal Sublime Text UI, nothing native.

  - **ApplySyntax** lets you tell it "treat files that look like this as
    that language" through a menu; it opens your web browser for its help
    page, same as any link would.

  - **ColorConverter** converts a color value you've typed (like a hex
    code) between formats using a built-in color-math library. Pure
    calculation, no outside calls.

  - **Google Spell Check** sends your selected text to Google's public
    spell-check service over the internet and shows you the suggestions.
    A normal, watchable web request.

  - **PHP Getters and Setters** looks at the PHP class you're editing and
    generates boilerplate getter/setter methods for you, picking which
    ones from an on-screen menu.

  - **EasyDiff** compares two pieces of text using your operating
    system's ordinary `diff` command-line tool and shows you the result.

  - **Bracketeer** handles smart bracket/quote insertion and matching
    while you type. Pure text editing logic.

  - **ExportHtml** turns your current file into a styled HTML or RTF
    document; it can optionally hand that off to an external tool to make
    a PDF, which is a normal background program call.

  - **Simple FTP Deploy** uploads your file to an FTP server using
    Python's own standard, fully scriptable FTP support -- no separate
    FTP application involved.

  - **RawLineEdit** lets you toggle between seeing a line "as written" or
    "as processed." Just a display toggle plus a help-page link.

  - **RegReplace** runs find-and-replace rules you've defined in your
    settings against the current file. Pure text substitution.

  - **RSpec** runs your Ruby test suite by using Sublime Text's own
    built-in "run a command and show me the output" feature (the same
    feature every build system uses) -- fully watchable by design.

  - **Clickable URLs** makes web links in your text clickable. Just
    highlighting and opening links.

  - **MarkdownTOC** builds a table of contents from the headings in your
    Markdown file; it can optionally look something up on GitHub over the
    internet for formatting link slugs.

  - **StringEncode** encodes/decodes selected text (base64, URL-encoding,
    etc); one of its options calls an online conversion service, ordinary
    web request.

  - **RainbowBrackets** colors matching brackets different colors as you
    type. Purely visual highlighting.

  - **xpath** lets you run an XPath query against an XML/HTML file you
    have open and shows the matches, using a standard Python XML library.

  - **GhostText** lets a web browser extension send text from a browser
    text box into Sublime Text to edit, by opening an ordinary local
    network connection that Sublime Text's own script owns and listens
    on -- not a native window.

  - **TabsExtra** adds extra tab-management features (closing groups of
    tabs, etc), with a web link for its documentation.

  - **NeoVintageous** brings Vim-style keyboard editing to Sublime Text.
    It can run shell commands the way Vim does, and it makes one tiny,
    instant Windows system call to ask "what's the current text
    encoding" -- again, an instant lookup, not a popup window.

  - **BootstrapAutocomplete** just offers autocomplete suggestions for
    Bootstrap CSS framework class names, from a fixed built-in list.

  - **Open URL** finds and opens URLs in your text, checking that they're
    reachable over the internet first.

  - **Wrap Plus** reflows/wraps paragraph text to a chosen line width.
    Pure text manipulation, no outside calls at all.

  - **Console Exec** runs whatever text you've selected as a shell
    command and shows the output. A direct, watchable program launch.

  - **CFML** adds language support for ColdFusion/CFML files, with menus,
    an internet connection for some lookups, and a help link. Nothing
    native.

  - **SSH Config** helps you open and edit your SSH configuration files.
    Plain file reading and writing.

  - **ScopeHunter** shows you technical info about the text style/scope
    under your cursor, useful for theme authors, with a help-page link.

  - **Laravel Goto** helps you jump to Laravel framework files (views,
    routes) from a menu; it can optionally run the framework's own
    command-line tool.

  - **ColorHints** shows a little color swatch next to CSS color names
    and codes, using built-in lookup tables. No outside calls.

  - **RustFmt** runs the standard Rust code formatter on your file
    through Sublime Text's own built-in command-runner feature.

  - **FuzzyFileNav** is a quick file-browser popup for jumping between
    files; like Package Control, it makes one tiny instant Windows call
    to check a file's attributes, not a popup window.

  - **OpenAI completion** sends your prompt to OpenAI's servers over the
    internet and inserts the reply into your file. Ordinary web request.

  - **CNC Sinumerik** adds support for a specific machine-tool
    programming language, and can run an external toolchain program for
    it.

  - **XSL** creates a new file from a template. Just reads a bundled
    template and inserts it -- no outside calls.

  - **AutoSetSyntax** automatically picks the right syntax highlighting
    for a file based on rules, some of which can be updated over the
    internet.

  - **Sort Lines (Numerically)** sorts the lines in your file in true
    numeric order (so "2" comes before "10") using a bundled sorting
    library. Pure text operation.

**Bottom line for this pass:** out of 182 genuinely popular, currently
maintained packages, 46 aren't real plugins, 39 never updated their code
to work with the current engine, and every one of the 97 that were real,
working plugins can already be fully operated the normal way -- none of
them popped open one of those un-drivable native system windows.
Combined with everything looked at earlier in the whole campaign, only
two packages, out of the entire popular-and-maintained catalog, were ever
flagged as possibly needing something extra: a color picker (ColorPicker)
and another package's optional native color picker setting (ColorHelper)
-- both because they open the operating system's own color-picker window.

**Correction, tested for real (2026-09-14): that flag doesn't hold up
either.** Triggering the picker the normal way (through Sublime's own
command) does freeze Sublime -- the package's own code waits for the
picker to close before doing anything else, on the same thread Sublime
uses for everything. But that's a fact about how the package calls it,
not about whether the window itself can be reached. Launched the exact
same picker program directly, on its own, completely outside Sublime,
and drove it for real: read its real on-screen controls, typed a new
color into its text box, clicked its OK button, and watched it close
correctly -- a full, working round trip, using only tools already in
the kit (no new server, nothing package-specific). So the real fix for
ColorPicker/ColorHelper isn't a dedicated MCP -- it's calling the picker
program directly instead of through Sublime's blocking command, then
driving the resulting window the same way any other native window would
be driven, and finally writing the chosen color back into the file
normally.

**Final answer for the whole campaign:** across the entire current,
popular Package Control catalog -- not a sample, the full list, filtered
down to packages people actually install and keep updated -- **zero
packages need a dedicated MCP server.** Everything real and current is
reachable with what already exists here. Packages below the popularity/
recency bar were deliberately not looked at, per instruction -- this is
a statement about the packages people actually use today, not the
entire historical catalog.


### 2026-09-14 (later still): live install-and-exercise bug hunt, in progress

Different task from everything above: the user asked to actually install
and run real packages live, one at a time, looking for genuine bugs worth
filing -- not just reading source. Target list: the ~40 substantive real
plugins out of the 182-package shortlist (the trivial one-file config
wrappers and non-plugins were already excluded). Only writing something
up here if it's a real, reproducible bug with real before/after evidence.

**A File Icon -- real bug found, live, by accident during normal use.**
What happened: the package's "revert" command (the only command it has)
was run, then shortly after, the package was removed the normal way. A
few seconds later, Sublime Text's own console showed a real crash
message on its own, with a full error trace, coming from code inside A
File Icon that had no idea the package had just been removed:

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../A File Icon.sublime-package/plugin.py", line 35, in remove_overlay
  File ".../A File Icon.sublime-package/core/settings.py", line 24, in add_listener
  File "...\sublime.py", line 1199, in load_resource
    raise FileNotFoundError(f'resource "{name}" not found')
FileNotFoundError: resource "Packages/A File Icon/A File Icon.sublime-settings" not found
```

In plain terms: when you run A File Icon's "revert" command, it doesn't
clean up right away -- it schedules some follow-up cleanup work to
happen a fraction of a second later, in the background. Part of that
follow-up work is: "go re-read my own settings file." That's fine if the
package is still there when the follow-up work actually runs. But if the
package gets removed (by a normal uninstall, or by Package Control
upgrading it to a new version, which also removes-then-reinstalls) in
that same short window, the follow-up work tries to read a settings file
that no longer exists, and the whole thing crashes with an ugly error in
the console instead of failing quietly. This is a real, timing-dependent
bug in the package's own cleanup code, not anything about how it was
invoked -- and it's realistic to hit by accident, exactly as it was hit
here: run the "revert" command, then remove or upgrade the package
shortly after. Repro steps for whoever files this: install "A File
Icon," run its "AFI: Revert filetype changes" command from the command
palette, then immediately remove or upgrade the package before a couple
of seconds pass -- the console shows the exact traceback above. The fix
on the package's end would be wrapping that follow-up settings reload in
a try/except (the same pattern the package already uses in a couple of
other places) instead of leaving it bare.

**ApplySyntax -- a second, different bug read from the source and set up
to test live, but the live confirmation didn't finish (see blocker
below).** Reading the package's own code found a real inconsistency: it
has a setting called "reraise_exceptions" whose whole documented purpose
is "keep errors from showing up in the console unless you turn this on."
The package actually honors that setting in two of its three ways of
matching a file to a syntax (its "glob pattern" matching and its
"custom function" matching both correctly hide their errors by default).
But its third way of matching -- plain regular-expression rules, like
"if the file's first line looks like this pattern, use this syntax" --
has no such protection at all. A broken regular expression in a user's
own syntax rule (an easy mistake -- unbalanced brackets/parentheses is a
one-character typo) will throw a real, uncaught error every single time
a file is opened or saved, regardless of the "reraise_exceptions"
setting, which is supposed to prevent exactly that. This was set up for
a live test (installed the package, wrote a syntax rule with a
deliberately broken regular expression, created a test file to open) but
the actual live confirmation -- watching the real error happen when the
file opens -- did not complete before the environment blocker below hit,
so this is not yet confirmed the same way the A File Icon bug is. Worth
someone re-running: install ApplySyntax, add a rule like `{"name": "x",
"syntax": "Packages/Text/Plain text.tmLanguage", "rules": [{"first_line":
"(unclosed["}]}` to the "syntaxes" list in ApplySyntax's User settings,
then open any real file and check the console.

**Blocker hit partway through package 2 of ~40: the shared Sublime
instance's main thread got stuck.** This has nothing to do with either
package above -- while working through ApplySyntax, Sublime Text's main
thread stopped responding to anything (every kind of call started timing
out: running commands, running Python, even just listing installed
commands), and a live health check confirmed why: the main thread was
stuck cycling inside the GhostShell terminal package's own screen-
drawing code (`ai_terminal.py`, `_build_text_and_regions`), not inside
anything related to package testing. It wasn't a hard freeze -- Sublime
kept a faint pulse (about one tick every several seconds instead of five
times a second) -- but nothing could reliably get a response out of it
for many minutes straight, including a plain "list installed commands"
call, which should be near-instant. Waited it out for several minutes
with the health check confirming the same stuck state the whole time; it
did not clear on its own in that window. This looks like the same class
of shared-instance disruption noted earlier in this log (multiple
sessions/terminal tabs sharing one live Sublime Text process can starve
each other), just triggered by something else this time, not by a
package under test. Cleaned up ApplySyntax's test files directly from
disk (bypassing Sublime entirely, since it wasn't responding) rather than
leave them behind; the package itself had already disappeared from disk
on its own sometime during the stuck period, so there was nothing left
to formally uninstall through Package Control.

**Status update: Sublime reattached and confirmed healthy; resumed.** The
freeze really was unrelated to package testing -- a render-throughput
problem in the terminal plugin itself, fixed by detaching and
reattaching that tab. Went back to finish confirming ApplySyntax and hit
a second, separate wrinkle: after everything that happened during the
freeze, Sublime's own package loader stopped picking up ApplySyntax
specifically -- installing it (twice, clean each time) no longer made
its Python code actually load, even though the exact same install step
worked immediately for a different package (Bracketeer) tried right
after, which rules out a general "nothing new loads" problem. This looks
like leftover, one-off confusion in this session's package index from
the earlier freeze, tied to ApplySyntax specifically (it was the package
being installed/edited right when the freeze happened), not a bug in
ApplySyntax and not something a plain reinstall could clear -- it would
likely need Sublime itself restarted to fully resolve, which wasn't done
here. So: **the ApplySyntax finding stands as source-confirmed only, not
live-confirmed** -- the code-level evidence (one of its three matching
methods missing the error-suppression its two siblings have) is solid
and specific enough to act on, but the live "watch it actually throw"
step could not be completed this session. Worth a plain reinstall-and-
retry after a normal Sublime restart if someone wants the live capture
too. Test settings file, test file, and the installed package were all
cleaned up either way.

Continuing through the remaining packages now.

**Bracketeer -- clean, no bug.** Read its bracket-jump command
(`bracketeer_goto`), which reads the character one position to the left
of the cursor before deciding where to jump -- a plausible crash if the
cursor is at the very start of the file (position 0, so "one to the
left" is position -1). Tested live: put the cursor at position 0 in a
real buffer and ran the "jump left" command. No crash -- Sublime Text's
own `substr()` quietly returns nothing for an out-of-range position
instead of raising an error, so the command just does nothing instead of
failing. A reasonable worry that turned out not to be a real bug.

**AutoSetSyntax -- real, confirmed bug: the package can fail to load at
all, for every single feature, not just the one it's trying to work
around.** This one wasn't even part of the planned edge-case test --
installing the package fresh and opening one ordinary file (an empty
text file) was enough to trigger it immediately, live, with a full
error trace:

```
File ".../AutoSetSyntax.sublime-package/boot.py", line 32, in <module>
File ".../AutoSetSyntax.sublime-package/boot.py", line 23, in bypass_pydantic_version_check
File "./python3.8/pathlib.py", line 1229, in read_bytes
FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory:
  '...\\Lib\\python38\\pydantic\\version.py'
```

In plain terms: AutoSetSyntax ships a small workaround (its own code
comment links to the exact GitHub issue it's patching) for a known
conflict with a library called "pydantic" that Package Control itself
carries internally. The workaround's very first move, before anything
else in the package even starts, is to open and rewrite one specific
file inside Package Control's own internal folder. That file genuinely
wasn't there in this environment when AutoSetSyntax was installed
(confirmed directly: Package Control's internal library folder had no
"pydantic" folder in it at all at that moment). The workaround has no
fallback for that -- it only handles "Package Control isn't installed at
all" (that case is wrapped safely), not "Package Control is installed
but doesn't have this particular internal file yet." Because this code
runs immediately when the package's main file loads, and nothing catches
the error, the *entire* package fails to load -- not just the specific
pydantic-related feature, everything, syntax detection included, the
thing the package is actually for. Confirmed reproducible: happened
identically and immediately on a fresh install with no special setup.
Repro for whoever files this: install AutoSetSyntax fresh in an
environment where Package Control's own bundled "pydantic" library
folder isn't present yet, and watch the console right after install --
the traceback above appears immediately, before the package does
anything else. The fix on the package's end is straightforward: wrap
that file read/write in a try/except the same way the "is Package
Control even installed" check already is, so a missing file just skips
the workaround instead of taking down the whole package.

**Methodology note, applies going forward:** installing a package
through this session's install tool does not automatically finish
resolving its non-package Python library dependencies (things like
"pydantic" that several packages share, installed separately from the
package itself) -- that needs Package Control's own "Satisfy Libraries"
step run explicitly afterward. Found this the hard way on the very next
package below, which looked broken because of the missing library, not
because of anything in the package's own code. Will run "Satisfy
Libraries" after every install from here on to avoid false alarms.

**BootstrapAutocomplete -- real, confirmed bug (after correctly ruling
out the dependency red herring above).** Its autocomplete list is
chosen by a "versions" setting (which Bootstrap version(s) to offer
completions for). Give it a version string that doesn't match any of
the Bootstrap versions the package actually ships data for -- a typo is
all it takes, e.g. "5" typed as "5x" -- and every single autocomplete
attempt in a matching file throws a real, uncaught error instead of
just not offering suggestions:

```
File ".../BootstrapAutocomplete.sublime-package/plugin/completion.py", line 15, in load_db
    return DbModel.model_validate_json(sublime.load_binary_resource(...))
FileNotFoundError: resource "Packages\BootstrapAutocomplete\db\not-a-real-version.json" not found
```

Confirmed live and directly: set "versions" to a made-up value, called
the package's real completion-lookup function the same way Sublime
Text's autocomplete would, and got the exact traceback above -- not
guessed, watched it happen. Because of how the lookup function is
cached internally, this doesn't just happen once -- it happens on every
single autocomplete request for as long as the bad setting is in place,
which in real use means constant console spam every time the user types
in a matching file. Repro for whoever files this: set
`"versions": "not-a-real-version"` (or any Bootstrap version string that
doesn't exist) in BootstrapAutocomplete's settings, open a file the
package applies to, and trigger autocomplete -- the traceback above
appears immediately. The fix on the package's end: catch the "no such
version file" case in its version-loading function and either ignore
that version or show a clear one-time settings warning, instead of
letting the raw file-not-found error escape on every keystroke.

**CFML -- clean, no bug found in the time spent.** Large, well-organized
package (76 source files). Installed it, opened a deliberately broken
CFML file (a component definition truncated mid-attribute, never
closed), put the cursor at the very end of that broken file, and
triggered autocomplete right there -- the exact "malformed input at the
edge of the buffer" case most likely to trip up a parser. No crash, no
console error. Not an exhaustive audit of all 76 files given time, but
the real edge case tried came back clean.

**CNC Sinumerik -- real, confirmed bug: renumbering CNC code lines
crashes on a specific kind of blank last line.** Its "renumber blocks"
command walks each line of the file character by character to skip
leading spaces/tabs, then looks at the next character to decide what
kind of line it is. If a line is *entirely* spaces or tabs with nothing
after it -- most likely to happen on the very last line of a file that
doesn't end with a newline -- the skip-whitespace step walks right off
the end of the line's text and the very next character lookup fails for
real:

```
File ".../CNC Sinumerik.sublime-package/gcode/commands/blockno.py", line 113, in renumber_region
    while line[i] in ' \t':
IndexError: string index out of range
```

Confirmed live and directly: built a real buffer via the actual
installed package's own command class ("N10 G01 X10" followed by a
final line that's just three spaces, no trailing newline), ran the real
renumber logic on it, and got the exact crash above from the real
installed code. Repro for whoever files this: in a CNC Sinumerik file,
make sure the very last line is whitespace-only with no newline after
it, select the whole file (or leave nothing selected, which renumbers
the whole file by default), and run "CNC Sinumerik: Renumber Blocks" --
the traceback above appears immediately, and the file is left
unmodified since the crash happens before anything is written back. The
fix on the package's end: check `i < len(line)` in that while loop (or
equivalently, strip trailing whitespace before deciding whitespace-only
vs not) instead of assuming every line has a non-blank character to stop
on.

**Clickable URLs -- real, confirmed bug: turning off its file-size limit
the obvious way breaks URL detection completely.** The package has a
safety setting, "max_file_size," that skips scanning files above a
certain size so it doesn't slow down huge files. If someone tries to
turn that limit off by setting it to `null` (a completely natural thing
to try, since `null`/`none` commonly means "no limit" in other tools),
every single URL scan -- which runs on opening a file, switching to a
file, and every pause while typing -- throws a real error instead of
just scanning without a limit:

```
File ".../Clickable URLs.sublime-package/clickable_urls.py", line 105, in urls_for
    if view.size() > UrlHighlighter.settings.get('max_file_size'):
TypeError: '>' not supported between instances of 'int' and 'NoneType'
```

Confirmed live: set `"max_file_size": null` in the package's settings,
then called its own real URL-scanning function on a real buffer
containing a real URL, using the actual installed code -- got the exact
error above, not guessed. In real use this means URL highlighting,
clickable phantoms, and click-to-open all silently stop working the
moment someone tries this, with an error spamming the console on nearly
every keystroke and every file switch, worse than doing nothing.
Otherwise this package is unusually well-written for its size (real
comments explaining race-condition handling, a semaphore around its
shared caches, careful settings-change handling) -- this is the one gap
in an otherwise careful design. Repro for whoever files this: set
`"max_file_size": null` in Clickable URLs' settings, open any file
containing a URL, and check the console -- the traceback above appears
right away. The fix on the package's end: treat a `null`/missing
`max_file_size` as "no limit" explicitly (skip the size check entirely)
instead of comparing directly against whatever the setting returns.

**CoffeeScript -- clean, no bug found (the obvious candidate didn't pan
out).** Went in expecting a crash from running the compile command with
the real `coffee` compiler not installed (true of this machine) --
other platforms would hit a raw, uncaught crash from Python's own
process-launcher when a program doesn't exist. On Windows specifically,
though, the package runs the compiler through the shell (`shell=True`),
so a missing program becomes a normal "not recognized as a command"
error message instead of a crash -- confirmed live, no exception either
way. An accidental save, not a designed one, but real users on Windows
won't hit a crash from this path either way.

**ColorConverter -- real, confirmed bug: converting a color from the
right-click menu uses the wrong cursor position when there's no mouse
event, and silently does nothing instead of converting the color under
the cursor.** Reading the source found a real typo: the helper that
figures out which point in the file to work on has two paths -- one for
when you right-click (uses the click position, correct), and one for
when there's no click, which is supposed to fall back to the cursor
position. That fallback path accidentally returns a yes/no true-or-false
value instead of the actual position number (a stray comparison,
`selections[0].begin() >= 0`, where it should just be
`selections[0].begin()`). Since "true" behaves like the number 1 in
Python, this makes the command silently operate on whatever's at
*character position 1 of the file*, no matter where the real cursor is.

Confirmed live: put a real, valid color (`#ff0000`) in a test buffer,
put the cursor directly inside it, and ran the same command the
right-click menu runs when triggered without a real mouse click (which
happens for things like command-palette invocation or a custom
keybinding) -- the buffer came back completely unchanged. The color
under the cursor was never touched, because the command was actually
looking at an unrelated character elsewhere in the file and, finding no
color there, silently gave up (its own error handling swallows the
failure into a vague "that does not seem to be a color" status message,
so there's no crash to notice -- just nothing happening). Repro for
whoever files this: bind or trigger `color_convert_context` (or
`color_convert_copy_context`) any way that doesn't produce a real mouse
click -- Command Palette, a custom keybinding, calling the command
directly -- with the cursor sitting on a real color elsewhere in the
file; the color is left unconverted. The fix on the package's end: drop
the `>= 0` comparison so the fallback path returns the actual cursor
position, not a boolean.

**ColorHints -- real, confirmed bug: its own sidebar "Show Color Hints"
command can never actually run.** Every Sublime Text command that edits
a file gets called by Sublime with a special internal "edit" token as
its first argument, automatically, every time, no exceptions -- that's
just how the API works. This particular command's `run` method was
written without that first parameter at all, expecting only the
arguments the sidebar menu sends it ("which files did you click"). The
result: the moment Sublime tries to call it for real, its automatic
"edit" token collides with the real argument, and it fails outright:

```
TypeError: run() got multiple values for argument 'paths'
```

Confirmed by simulating the exact call Sublime itself makes for this
command (not a guess about the API -- reproduced the same call
internally) -- got the exact error above every time, with the real
installed code. In plain terms: this command is completely non-
functional as shipped; anyone who right-clicks a file in the sidebar and
picks "Show Color Hints" (its only real entry point) gets nothing but a
silent failure in the console, never the actual feature. Repro for
whoever files this: right-click a file in Sublime's sidebar with
ColorHints installed and choose "Show Color Hints" -- check the console
right after, the traceback above appears immediately, and the feature
visibly does nothing. The fix on the package's end: add the missing
`edit` parameter to the method's signature (`def run(self, edit,
paths):`), matching every other text command in the package.

**Methodology note, second occurrence:** the same package-loading quirk
from ApplySyntax earlier hit again here -- a freshly installed package
that Sublime's resource system can clearly see (its files are findable,
its settings load fine) but whose actual Python code never gets
registered as importable, even after re-triggering with the
ignored-packages toggle and a long wait. Confirmed genuinely independent
of the earlier main-thread freeze (that was hours of wall-clock time
and several clean successful installs ago). Not spending more time
chasing the cause a second time -- treating it the same way: the source
finding stands on the code alone, marked as not live-confirmed, and
moving on rather than blocking the rest of the list on it.

**EasyDiff -- real bug, source-confirmed, live confirmation blocked by
the loader quirk above.** Its "Compare Both" command reads a
module-level variable that's supposed to hold whatever was chosen with
"Set Left Side" earlier. If someone runs "Compare Both" without ever
having run "Set Left Side" first -- a completely plausible first-use
mistake, or just clicking the wrong menu item -- that variable is still
empty, and the comparison code immediately tries to look up a key inside
it as if it were already filled in. That would throw a real
`TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable` the moment "Compare
Both" runs before "Set Left Side" has ever been used. Could not get the
live traceback this session because the package never finished loading
(see the note above), but the code path is unambiguous: `LEFT` starts as
`None` at the top of the file, `EasyDiffCompareBothCommand.get_left()`
returns it unchanged when nothing's been set, and the very next line
indexes into it as a dict. Worth a quick re-check by whoever files this:
install EasyDiff, run "Compare Both" (not "Compare Left/Right") as the
very first thing without ever running "Set Left Side," and check the
console.

**EditorConfig -- clean, no bug found.** Deliberately fed it a
`.editorconfig` file with garbage values (`indent_size = not_a_number`,
`trim_trailing_whitespace = maybe`) and opened a real file under it.
Called its real settings-applying code directly on that file and
watched what it did: it quietly ignored the bad indent size (left tab
size at the normal default of 4) instead of crashing, and just skipped
the equally-nonsensical trim setting. Careful, defensive as shipped.

**ExportHtml -- untestable this session, no strong bug candidate found
either way.** Same loading quirk as ApplySyntax and EasyDiff above hit
again -- installed cleanly but its Python code never became callable
this session. Unlike those two, a real source read of its main file
(1,128 lines) didn't turn up a specific, confident bug candidate to
write up as source-confirmed-only, so this one is genuinely untested
rather than "found but not yet proven live." Worth a fresh look outside
this session if someone wants it covered.

**FuzzyFileNav -- real, confirmed bug: showing the true-case name of a
drive root crashes on Windows.** The package has a small Windows-only
helper that fixes up a path's letter casing (Windows file paths aren't
case sensitive, but the package wants to display them with their real,
on-disk capitalization). It builds this by splitting the path into
folder-name pieces and looking at each piece's last character. That
breaks for exactly one kind of path: the bare root of a drive, like
`C:\`, which splits into the drive letter and one completely empty
piece -- and asking an empty piece of text for "its last character"
fails immediately:

```
IndexError: string index out of range
```

Couldn't route this through Sublime itself this session (same loading
quirk as ApplySyntax/EasyDiff/ExportHtml above -- installed cleanly but
never became callable inside Sublime this time), so instead pulled this
exact function's code straight out of the real installed
`.sublime-package` file, confirmed it's byte-for-byte identical to what
was read from source, and ran it for real in a real Windows Python
process -- got the exact crash above. This path is reachable for real
users: it's called whenever the package shows a Sublime project's
folder list, so any project that includes a folder set to a bare drive
root (`C:\`, `D:\`, etc. -- not unusual for someone who wants a whole
drive as a project folder) would hit this the moment that folder list
is shown. Repro for whoever files this: add a project folder that's a
bare drive root, and trigger whatever FuzzyFileNav view lists project
folders -- the traceback above appears immediately. The fix on the
package's end: skip empty path pieces (or just return the path
unchanged when normpath produces one) instead of assuming every piece
has at least one character.

**GhostText -- real, confirmed bug: the local server it opens will crash
its connection handler on any incomplete message, from anything that
can reach it, not just the real browser extension.** GhostText works by
opening a small, unauthenticated local web server that a browser
extension talks to -- first a plain HTTP request, then a live
WebSocket connection carrying JSON messages back and forth. When the
very first message comes in on that WebSocket connection, the code
assumes it will always contain a "url" field and reads it directly,
with no check that it's actually there.

Confirmed live, for real, end to end -- not simulated: installed the
package, let it open its real local server, made a real HTTP request to
get the real port it randomly picked, opened a real WebSocket
connection to that port (the same handshake any browser extension
would do), and sent the simplest possible incomplete message, `{}`
(valid JSON, just missing the fields it expects). The real, live server
thread crashed immediately with a real traceback in the console:

```
Exception in thread Thread-28026:
  File ".../GhostText.sublime-package/GhostText.py", line 120, in on_message
KeyError: 'url'
```

Since this server has no authentication and no message validation,
anything on the same machine that can open a WebSocket to that port --
not just the official browser extension, but any other browser tab,
script, or program -- can trigger this the same way, and each time it
does, that connection's handler thread dies instead of giving a clean
error back. Repro for whoever files this: install GhostText, note the
port it reports (`GET http://localhost:4001/` returns it as JSON),
open a raw WebSocket connection to that port, and send `{}` as the
first message -- the traceback above appears immediately. The fix on
the package's end: check that `url`, `title`, and `text` are all
present (and handle it cleanly if not) before using them, the same way
it already correctly catches malformed JSON with `except ValueError`.

**Google Spell Check -- clean, no bug found.** Unusually careful code
for its size: replacements are applied back-to-front specifically so
earlier edits don't shift later ones, network failures are retried with
backoff and isolated per-selection so one bad region can't take down
the rest, and every edge case checked by hand (empty selections,
punctuation-only "words," case-only differences) turned out to already
be handled deliberately, with a comment explaining why.

**Indent XML -- real, confirmed bug: "Indent JSON" crashes on invalid
JSON, while its own sibling "Indent XML" handles the exact same kind of
mistake gracefully.** The package can reformat either XML or JSON.
Feeding it broken XML gives a clean, friendly message at the bottom of
the window ("Invalid XML: ...") -- that path is wrapped in real error
handling. Feeding broken JSON to the JSON side of the exact same
package does not go through any such handling at all, and crashes
outright:

```
File ".../Indent XML.sublime-package/indentxml.py", line 124, in indent
    parsed = json.loads(s)
json.decoder.JSONDecodeError: Expecting property name enclosed in
  double quotes: line 1 column 2 (char 1)
```

Confirmed live with the real installed command: selected clearly broken
JSON (`{invalid json, no closing`) and ran "Indent JSON" on it directly
-- got the exact crash above, using the real code, not a guess. Easy to
hit by accident -- select the wrong text, or catch a file mid-edit, and
run the command. Repro for whoever files this: select any invalid JSON
text and run "Indent JSON" (or "Auto Indent" on a `.json`-scoped file
with broken content) -- the traceback appears immediately, same as
above. The fix on the package's end: wrap `json.loads` in a try/except
the same way `parseString` already is on the XML side, and show an
equivalent friendly status message instead of letting it escape
uncaught.

**Laravel Goto -- clean on what was tested, not a full audit.** Pulled
its config-key and Blade-view path parsers out and fed them empty
strings, bare dots, and other malformed "click targets" directly (these
are pure text-parsing logic with no Sublime dependency, so they can be
tested standalone) -- no crash in any case, just a harmless nonsense
file path when the input made no sense, which is a reasonable failure
mode. Time-boxed rather than reading every one of its ~15 file-type
handlers; the two checked (config lookups, Blade view resolution)
held up.

**MarkdownEditing -- real, confirmed bug: emptying the list-bullet
setting (an easy way to try to turn off auto-bullets) crashes the
"insert task item" command outright.** The package lets you customize
which characters count as list bullets (`*`, `-`, `+` by default) via a
setting. Set that list to empty -- a natural thing to try if someone
wants to disable the feature -- and inserting a new GFM task checkbox
item crashes immediately, because the code assumes there's always at
least one bullet character to grab:

```
File ".../MarkdownEditing.sublime-package/plugins/lists.py", line 189, in run
    to_insert = "{} [ ]".format(bullets[0])
IndexError: list index out of range
```

Confirmed live with the real installed command: set
`"mde.list_indent_bullets": []` and ran "Insert Task List Item" -- got
the exact crash above. Worth noting for whoever looks at this: reading
the same file found that the indent/unindent list commands and the
bullet-type-switcher build a regex character class directly out of this
same setting (`"".join(re.escape(b) for b in bullets)`), which would
likely fail differently (an invalid, unterminated regex) under the same
empty-list setting -- flagging as a related but not independently
confirmed risk in the same file, worth a look alongside the main fix.
Repro for whoever files this: set the bullets setting to an empty list
and run "Insert Task List Item" -- the traceback above appears
immediately. The fix on the package's end: fall back to a default
bullet (or no-op) when the configured bullet list is empty, instead of
indexing into it unconditionally.

**MarkdownTOC -- real, confirmed bug: a broken custom find-and-replace
rule in its own settings crashes table-of-contents generation
entirely.** MarkdownTOC lets you define your own text replacement rules
(regular find-and-replace patterns) to clean up how heading text turns
into a link anchor. Nothing checks those patterns are valid regular
expressions before using them -- a single typo (an unclosed bracket, a
stray parenthesis) in one rule breaks TOC generation completely, not
just for that one heading:

```
re.error: unterminated character set at position 9
```

Same loading quirk as a few packages above hit again here, so this was
confirmed by pulling the real code straight out of the installed
`.sublime-package` and running it directly (with a minimal stand-in for
the one Sublime API call it needs at that point, which the crashing
code path never reaches) rather than through Sublime's command
dispatch -- the crash itself is 100% the real, unmodified installed
code. Repro for whoever files this: add a custom `id_replacements` rule
with a broken pattern like `"(unclosed["` in MarkdownTOC's settings,
then generate or update a table of contents on any file with a real
heading -- the traceback above appears immediately. The fix on the
package's end: wrap each user-supplied pattern's `re.sub` call in a
try/except and skip (or warn about) the one broken rule instead of
letting it take down the whole TOC generation.

**NeoVintageous -- inconclusive, not counted as a finding.** By far the
largest, most mature package tested this batch (a full Vim emulation, a
source tree that dwarfs everything else on the list). Repeat-search
with no prior search ("n" with nothing searched yet) came back clean.
Feeding it a command-line sequence (`:s/[/x/<CR>`, a substitute command
with a deliberately broken regex) on a freshly created buffer did throw
a real, repeating `KeyError: 'mode_unknown'` -- but the view it happened
on had never been through the package's own normal activation sequence
(its internal mode-tracking state was still completely unset), and
that's plausibly an artifact of creating and driving the buffer
programmatically in one synchronous burst rather than a real user
opening a file and typing -- not a controlled enough test to call a
confirmed bug either way. Didn't chase it further given how much of the
package (140KB in the main command file alone) was left unexplored;
flagging as a real "worth someone re-testing by hand, normally" rather
than writing it up as found.

**Open URL -- clean, no bug found.** Much larger and more careful than
its name suggests (a real deep-link system: `file.py:42`, `file.py:/regex/`,
line ranges, and more). The one real suspicion -- a user-supplied broken
regular expression reaching Sublime's own search function unguarded --
checked out fine on direct testing: Sublime's `view.find()` quietly
returns "no match" for an invalid pattern instead of raising, and the
package's own code already treats "no match" as a normal, handled case
with a fallback message. Extremely thorough inline comments throughout
explaining exactly why each edge case is handled the way it is.

**OpenAI completion -- real, confirmed bug: declining its "create cache
folder?" prompt crashes instead of just declining.** The first time it
needs a local cache folder that doesn't exist yet, it asks with a
normal Yes/Cancel dialog. Say no, and the code tries to record that
choice by calling a method that doesn't exist on the window object at
all:

```
w.set('')
AttributeError: 'Window' object has no attribute 'set'
```

Confirmed directly -- Sublime's real `Window` object genuinely has no
`set` method (checked live against the real API, not assumed), and this
is exactly what the package's own cache-folder code calls when a user
clicks "Cancel." A plain typo (almost certainly meant
`view.window().settings().set(...)` or similar), but it means the
"no, don't create that folder" path -- a completely normal, expected
choice -- crashes every time instead of just respecting the answer.

Reading the same small function found a second, related gap right next
to it, not independently live-confirmed but worth flagging together: if
reading the cached model fails (which is the normal, expected case the
first time the plugin is ever used, before any cache exists) it falls
back to `settings.get('assistants', None)[0]` with no guard -- an empty
or missing `assistants` list in the user's settings would crash the
same way the bullets/versions/id-replacement lists did in other
packages tested this session. Repro for the confirmed half: trigger
the "create cache folder?" prompt (delete the plugin's cache folder
under Sublime's cache path first, then run any completion command) and
click Cancel -- the traceback above appears immediately. The fix on the
package's end: replace the invalid `window().set(...)` call with
whatever the intended no-op actually was, and guard the
`assistants[0]` fallback the same way.

**PHP Getters and Setters -- real, confirmed bug: generating a
getter/setter for a short, underscore-prefixed property name crashes.**
The package strips a leading underscore convention (like `$_id`) before
building the function name, and checks a couple of extra characters to
decide exactly how to strip it -- but never checks the property name is
actually long enough to have those characters. A property name like
`$_a` (a single letter after the underscore -- a completely ordinary
short PHP property name, the kind used for loop counters or small
flags) is exactly two characters long, one short of what the check
needs:

```
File ".../PHP Getters and Setters.sublime-package/plugin.py", line 92, in getPartialFunctionName
    if name and name[0] == "_" and name[1].islower() and name[2].isupper():
IndexError: string index out of range
```

Confirmed live with the real installed code: built the package's own
`Variable` object for a property named `_a` and asked it for the
getter's function name, the same call the real "Generate Getter"
command makes -- got the exact crash above. A one-letter or bare
underscore property name is a real, easy thing to have in actual PHP
code, not a contrived case. Repro for whoever files this: put a
property like `private $_a;` in a PHP class and run "Generate Getter"
(or Setter, or Getter+Setter) on it -- the traceback above appears
immediately. The fix on the package's end: check `len(name) > 2` (or
use safer indexing) before looking at `name[1]`/`name[2]`.

**PlainTasks -- clean on what was reviewed, not a full audit.** Focused
on the most bug-prone area for a package like this: parsing the
embedded time-tracking annotations (`@lasted(...)`, `@total(...)`) back
out of task text to sum up project time. Found the code already has a
deliberate fix for the obvious gap -- when a time component wasn't
present in the original text (e.g. `@lasted()` with no duration), the
regex-extraction step would otherwise leave an empty value where a
number is expected, and there's an explicit find-and-replace patching
that to `"0"` before any number parsing happens. Time-boxed rather than
auditing the rest of two very large files (`commands.py` at 52KB,
`dates.py` at 34KB); the actual real test suite that ships with the
package is a better tool for the rest of it than continued manual
reading would be.

**RSpec -- real, confirmed bug: jumping between a Ruby file and its spec
file crashes on Windows specifically, whenever the quick guess
misses.** The "jump to the matching spec/source file" command has a
fast path that guesses the target path by find-and-replace, falling
back to a slower folder search only if that guess doesn't exist on
disk. One of the three guesses builds part of a regular expression
using `os.path.join("spec", "lib")` -- which is exactly the kind of
path-building helper you're supposed to use instead of hand-writing
separators. The problem: on Windows, that function joins with a
backslash, producing the text `spec\lib`, and a backslash in front of
an ordinary letter means something completely different inside a
regular expression than it does in a file path. `\l` isn't a valid
regex escape sequence at all:

```
re.sub(r"\b{}\b".format(os.path.join("spec", "lib")), "lib", file_path)
re.error: bad escape \l at position 6
```

Confirmed live on this real Windows machine with the real installed
code: called the command's own fallback path-guessing function
directly on an ordinary file path -- got the exact crash above,
immediately, every time that fallback path is reached. Repro for
whoever files this: on Windows, open a Ruby file whose spec (or vice
versa) isn't at one of the two fast-guess locations, and run "Toggle
Spec/Source" -- the traceback above appears as soon as the slower guess
list is tried. The fix on the package's end: build that particular
pattern with a literal `/` (regex doesn't care about OS path
separators, only real file-system calls do) instead of
`os.path.join`, the same way the adjacent two path guesses in the same
function already do.

**RainbowBrackets -- clean, no bug found.** One real suspicion from
reading the code -- a "remember the last bracket type" field used for
detecting rapid repeated keypresses that's never set in the class's
constructor -- turned out to be safe by construction: the very first
comparison that would touch it is guarded by a companion timestamp
that's deliberately initialized to zero, which makes that first
comparison always short-circuit before the unset field is ever
touched. Confirmed live: transformed a bracket pair to a different
bracket type, then transformed it again immediately -- both calls
worked correctly with no crash, matching what the source predicted.

**RawLineEdit -- plausible bug from source, not live-confirmed (loader
issue).** Its main toggle command decides what to do based on three
conditions, and reading them closely, an unsaved file that's never been
saved to disk (no file name at all) that isn't already in raw-line mode
doesn't match either of the first two conditions, and falls through to
the "turn raw-line mode on" branch anyway -- with no file name to read
the raw bytes from. Whether that actually crashes or is handled further
down couldn't be confirmed: this package hit the same install-then-
never-becomes-callable quirk noted a few times above, and unlike the
ones resolved that way earlier, this one's core logic needs too much
real view/dialog interaction to safely reconstruct outside Sublime the
way the pure-text-parsing bugs elsewhere were. Flagging as worth a
direct look (open a brand-new unsaved tab, don't save it, run "Toggle
Raw Line Edit") rather than writing it up as found or clearing it as
clean.

**RegReplace -- real bug, source-confirmed, not live-confirmed (same
loader issue).** The package's own regex-matching engine compiles the
user's find-pattern in two separate places for two different matching
modes. One of the two wraps that compile step in a real try/except and
reports a clean error through the package's own notification system.
The other -- the plain "find all matches" path, reached first and used
by the most basic replace operations -- compiles the exact same
user-supplied pattern with no error handling at all, a few thousand
characters earlier in the same file. A broken regex in a user's own
RegReplace rule would throw an uncaught error on that path while being
handled cleanly on its sibling path just because of which mode it
happens to run through. Same install-then-never-becomes-callable
quirk as a few packages above prevented a live capture of the actual
traceback this session, but the asymmetry itself is unambiguous
reading the two call sites side by side -- one has a `try:` immediately
around it, the other has none anywhere in its enclosing function.
Worth a direct check by whoever files this: add a RegReplace rule with
a deliberately broken "find" pattern and trigger a plain (non-plugin,
non-selection-scoped) replace on it.

**RustFmt -- clean, no bug found.** The real `rustfmt` compiler tool
happens to be installed on this machine, so this got a genuinely live,
end-to-end test rather than just source reading. Fed it deliberately
invalid Rust syntax through the real installed command -- it correctly
showed the user a real error dialog with the real compiler error text,
then raised a normal, expected exception matching exactly what the
source says it should do. No crash, no silent failure.

**SSH Config -- real, confirmed bug: customizing just one of its four
file paths in settings silently breaks the other three.** The package
ships default locations for four files (SSH config, SSHD config, known
hosts, authorized keys) as one settings block per operating system. If
someone wants to override just one of those four paths -- a completely
natural thing to try, since it's one JSON object -- Sublime Text's own
settings system doesn't merge nested objects, it replaces the whole
block. The user ends up with a settings block containing only the one
path they meant to change, and the other three "Open X" commands break
immediately:

```
File ".../SSH Config.sublime-package/main.py", line 17, in get_file_location
    return expandvars(setting[identifier])
KeyError: 'sshd_config'
```

Confirmed live with the real installed code: set a settings override
that customizes only the Windows SSH-config path (leaving the other
three keys out, exactly as someone would if they only meant to change
one), then asked the package for the SSHD config location the same way
its own "Open SSHD Config File" command does -- got the exact crash
above. Repro for whoever files this: in SSH Config's user settings, set
`"default_file_locations"` to an object containing only one platform
and only one file key (e.g. just `windows.ssh_config`), then run any of
the other three "Open ... File" commands -- the traceback above appears
immediately. The fix on the package's end: merge the user's override
into the shipped defaults key-by-key instead of trusting Sublime's
settings system to do it, or read each file key with a safe fallback
instead of direct indexing.

### 2026-09-24: xpath#47 PR (explicit one-off exception to the report-only rule)
Donald asked to fix Keith Hall's code after he offered a PR (Donald doesn't use Copilot). Flagged
the conflict with the standing "report bugs, never patch" rule via AskUserQuestion; Donald confirmed
"Yes, fix it and open a PR" -- a deliberate override, not a repeal (memory updated with the exception
criteria: only when the maintainer has explicitly invited a patch AND Donald confirms). Forked
rawsp33d/sublime-xpath to dpc00/sublime-xpath, branched fix-entity-not-defined from upstream/master.

Root cause confirmed empirically (not from memory): lxml's target-parser interface
(etree.XMLParser(target=...)) never expands internal-DTD general entities, on the real lxml 6.1.3/
libxml2 2.11.9 installed here -- tried resolve_entities/load_dtd/no_network/dtd_validation, none
worked; recover=True avoids the crash but silently drops the entity's text to empty (worse). Plain
etree.fromstring() on the identical bytes works fine, confirming this is specifically a target-parser
limitation, not a general lxml/libxml2 issue.

Fix: on "Entity not defined", regex-extract simple internal-DTD <!ENTITY name "value"> declarations
and retry once with &name; refs substituted, PADDED/TRUNCATED TO EXACTLY THE SAME LENGTH as the
reference so every other node's recorded character offset (the whole point of this custom parser)
stays exactly correct. Parameter entities (%) and external entities (SYSTEM/PUBLIC) deliberately left
unresolved (XXE-safety, and % entities need real DTD semantics this doesn't attempt). Genuinely
undefined entities still raise the ORIGINAL error unchanged.

Verified live in Sublime (eval_python against the real installed lxml, loading the patched file
directly): original repro fixed; exact-length round trip with byte-exact downstream position
preserved; chunk sizes 1/2/3/5/7 incl. splitting "&e;" across a chunk boundary; position_offset
respected; over-long value truncates; CDATA "&e;" left literal; undefined entity still raises;
undefined general entity next to an unrelated parameter entity still raises. Added 7 new assertions
to tests.py (sublime_lxml_internal_dtd_entity_tests) matching the file's existing style.

Ran the REAL, complete existing test suite (not just my new checks) inside actual Sublime Text via
a temporary dev-package junction (Packages\XpathPRTest -> the git branch checkout) so
window.run_command('run_xpath_tests') exercises the genuine package machinery end to end -- passed
with zero regressions. To remove any command-name-collision ambiguity, also uninstalled the real
Package-Control 'xpath' package (which had been reinstalled earlier just to pull the lxml library)
and re-ran the full suite with ONLY the patched dev package present -- still 100% pass. Junction then
deleted (verified LinkType=Junction before delete, so only the link was removed, not the target);
lxml library left installed (harmless); ST back to the 6 baseline PC packages.

PR opened: https://github.com/rawsp33d/sublime-xpath/pull/48 (dpc00:fix-entity-not-defined ->
rawsp33d:master), body explains root cause, scope/limitations, full verification steps, and the
AI-assisted-testing context per Donald's own reply style on the issue thread.

## SubCalc (2026-09-24)

- Found: the released `.sublime-package` has no `.python-version` file at all (confirmed by listing the actual installed zip), so Package Control loads it into the legacy Python 3.3 plugin host. SubCalc.py uses Python 3.6+/3.7+ syntax (PEP 526 variable annotations, `from __future__ import annotations`, `dataclass`, PEP 585 builtin generics), so the module fails outright with `SyntaxError: invalid syntax` on import -- the entire package is non-functional for every real Package Control install.
- Root cause confirmed via GitHub: `.gitattributes` has `/.python-version export-ignore`, misclassifying it as a dev-only file (like `.pre-commit-config.yaml`, `pyproject.toml`, `tests/`) when it's actually required at runtime for plugin-host selection. The GitHub repo itself has the file; only the exported release archive is missing it -- a clone-based test would never have caught this.
- Filed https://github.com/vonbehr/SubCalc/issues/1.
- Since the package never imports, there is no further live functionality to test. Uninstalled, verified `Packages\` and `Packages\User\` clean.

## GitHubPullRequest (2026-09-24)

- Targeted review at the two highest-value attack surfaces for a tool that shells out and renders attacker-influenced content (PR comments from anyone who can comment):
  - `gh.py`: every `gh` invocation goes through `subprocess.run(args_list, ...)` -- no `shell=True` anywhere, so no shell injection; explicit timeout; correct `--raw-field` vs `--field` distinction to avoid gh's own type-coercion footguns (documented in a comment).
  - `render.py`'s `html_to_minihtml`: GitHub's server-rendered comment HTML (`bodyHTML`) is sanitized via a real streaming `HTMLParser` subclass with a strict tag allowlist (not a regex-based sanitizer, avoiding that whole bug class), `<img>`/`<script>`/`<style>` neutralized, and -- the standout finding -- `_safe_anchor()` explicitly strips the `href` from any link whose scheme isn't http(s), specifically because the plugin's own internal actions (resolve/discard/edit a draft, etc.) are dispatched through `subl:githubpullrequest?...` hrefs, and an attacker-controlled PR comment could otherwise forge one of those to trigger a real action via a crafted link. Traced the dispatch sink in plugin.py's `_handle_action`/`_open_external` and confirmed both paths are safe (unrecognized hrefs fall through to a second http(s)-only check before `webbrowser.open`).

Verified before filing: `_run_offline` is **dead code**, never called anywhere in the file -- only `_run_offline_subprocess` (a properly isolated child process with a real `proc.kill()` on timeout) is actually used for judging. No live bug.

Every invocation raises `NameError: name 'fn' is not defined`, silently swallowed by the method's own `except Exception as e: print(e)` -- the command does nothing, every time, with no visible error to the user. Reproduced directly by calling `CompileKspCliCommand().run()` against the installed package with a real open `.ksp` file, and isolated the exact line to confirm the `NameError`.

## RecentExplorer (2026-09-24)
- Installed live. A "project dashboard" that crawls all open project folders and lists source files sorted by modified/created time, with an interactive click-to-open dashboard view and an auto-refresh-on-save listener.
- Found and empirically confirmed a real, severe main-thread-block bug: `RecentExplorerOpenDashboardCommand` (a `WindowCommand`, guaranteed main thread) calls `render_project_dashboard()` directly, which does a full recursive `os.walk()` (plus an `os.stat()` per matching file) synchronously -- no `set_timeout_async`/threading anywhere in the file. Tested against a real, ordinary multi-repo workspace folder (`C:\Users\donal\projects`, not a pathological huge test fixture): the call blocked the main thread long enough that Sublime's own heartbeat monitor reported `likely_wedged: true` for 6+ seconds before recovering once the walk finished. Made significantly worse by `RecentExplorerListener.on_post_save_async`/`on_new_async`, which re-triggers this same synchronous walk on *every file save* while the dashboard tab is open (auto-refresh is on by default).
- Filed https://github.com/kushaagr/recent-explorer-sublime/issues/1.
- Test cleanup note: used a throwaway new window (diffed its ID against `sublime.windows()` before/after `new_window`, per the standing safety rule) with a temporary project folder set via `set_project_data`, rather than touching the active window/project. Closed the whole throwaway window afterward and confirmed only the original window remained.
- Uninstalled, verified `installed_packages`, `Packages\`, and `Packages\User\` clean.

## KodiDevKit (2026-09-24)
- Installed live. A large Kodi (XBMC) skin/addon development toolkit: XML skin parsing/validation, gettext translation tooling, ADB remote control, and an HTML validation-report system with its own bundled local HTTP server (`libs/reporting/server.py`) for click-to-open-in-editor navigation from report pages.
- Found and filed **two** separate, real bugs:
  1. **CSRF/CORS vulnerability, confirmed empirically end-to-end**: `libs/reporting/server.py`'s `/open` endpoint opens an arbitrary attacker-supplied file path in Sublime (and forcibly steals window focus / flashes the taskbar) with zero auth/origin/token checking, and sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` on every response. Bound to `localhost` only (not LAN-exposed), but localhost-only binding does **not** protect against browser-originated cross-origin requests, and the wildcard CORS header explicitly defeats the browser's own same-origin protection. Verified by starting the server (bypassing an unrelated missing-dependency issue with a minimal `lxml` stub -- see finding 2) and sending a plain `urllib.request` GET to `/open?file=...` with a spoofed `Origin: https://evil.example.com` header: request succeeded, response carried the wildcard CORS header, and the target file was opened as a real, focused view in the live Sublime session.
  2. **Dead-on-arrival dependency bug**: `dependencies.json` declares `lxml` as a dependency, but it never actually gets installed by Package Control on this real installation (`Lib/python38/` has `mdpopups`, `markupsafe`, `jinja2`, etc. from the same list, but no `lxml`). `libs/utils/xml.py` unconditionally imports `lxml.etree`, and since `libs/utils/__init__.py` re-exports from it and is imported by nearly every other module in the package (validation, reporting, skin parsing), the vast majority of KodiDevKit's functionality is unreachable -- confirmed directly via `importlib.import_module('KodiDevKit.libs.utils.xml')` raising `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'lxml'`. Same bug class as the `debugtools` dependency failures found earlier in RememberCommandPaletteInput/AmxxEditor.
- Filed https://github.com/MikeSiLVO/KodiDevKit/issues/5 (CORS/CSRF) and https://github.com/MikeSiLVO/KodiDevKit/issues/6 (missing lxml dependency).
- Test cleanup: stubbed `lxml`/`lxml.etree` in `sys.modules` only long enough to start the report server for the empirical CORS test, then removed the stub modules from `sys.modules` afterward so a genuinely lxml-dependent import elsewhere in the same session wouldn't be silently masked. Stopped the server, closed the probe view, deleted the temp probe file.
- Uninstalled, verified `installed_packages`, `Packages\`, and `Packages\User\` clean.

## Extractor (2026-09-24)
- Installed live. A structured-token extractor: pulls emails, URLs, IPs, hostnames, dates, UUIDs, MAC addresses, hex colors, credit-card numbers (Luhn-validated), API keys/secrets (AWS/Google/GitHub/Slack/JWT/PEM patterns), and more out of the active file/selection into a new plain-text file, plus a custom-regex extractor.
- Carefully-written package: bounded-repetition regexes throughout (no obviously vulnerable nested-quantifier patterns), explicit TLD/suffix curation to avoid false positives (e.g. distinguishing `main.py` from a hostname), Luhn validation for credit cards, deliberate 3.3-compatible syntax.
- Specifically checked the ReDoS bug class given how many regexes this package has, since it's the single densest concentration of hand-rolled patterns seen this campaign: extracted the most nested-quantifier-looking pattern (`PATH_RE`, `(?:[^\\/:*?"<>|\s,;]+\\?)*`-style) and ran it against adversarial inputs (long non-matching runs of thousands of characters) -- both completed in under 5ms, no catastrophic backtracking. Matches the briefing's running note that ReDoS hasn't panned out anywhere in this campaign despite repeated checking.
- Command runs entirely on the main thread (`WindowCommand.run()` -> `_emit()` synchronously), but operates on in-memory view text via linear-time regexes, not filesystem/subprocess work -- no realistic freeze risk found.
- No bug found. Uninstalled, verified `installed_packages`, `Packages\`, and `Packages\User\` clean.

## Json5Formatter (2026-09-24)
- Installed live. A JSON5/JSONC formatter with three commands: plain "Format" (local pure-Python parser), "Format as JSON5", and "Minify" (the latter two shell out to a real Python interpreter with the `json5` pip package).
- Found and empirically confirmed a real main-thread-block bug: `Json5FormatAsJson5Command`/`Json5MinifyCommand` (both `TextCommand`s, guaranteed main thread) call `_run()`, which does a synchronous `subprocess.Popen(...).communicate()` spawning a fresh `python`/`py` process per invocation -- no threading anywhere in the file. Measured directly: ~280ms for a trivial input (dominated by interpreter startup), and **1.36 seconds** for an ordinary ~118KB JSON file (2000-object array) -- a real, easily-reproducible UI freeze on totally normal file sizes. The plain "Format" command (`Json5FormatCommand`, using the local `lib/jsonc_formatter.format_json5()`) is unaffected -- no subprocess, no freeze.
- Filed https://github.com/RAMBOO1990/sublime-json5/issues/1.
- Uninstalled, verified `installed_packages`, `Packages\`, and `Packages\User\` clean.

## EDIBlime (2026-09-24)
- Installed live. A substantial EDI (Electronic Data Interchange) toolkit: beautify/minify/validate/repair/convert for EDIFACT, X12, TRADACOMS and HL7 dialects, with inline hint annotations, hover-help popups, envelope-integrity validation, and JSON/XML conversion.
- One of the most carefully engineered packages found this entire campaign -- explicitly designed around exactly the bug classes this campaign has been finding elsewhere: per-view state correctly keyed by `view.id()` (not the `view.file_name()`-collision bug found in Highlight Token), a debounce helper (`_debounce`) correctly keyed per-view (not the shared-function-object bug found in Telescope), an analysis cache keyed by `view.change_count()` so unchanged buffers are never re-parsed, and explicit `MAX_AUTO_SIZE`/`MAX_ENABLED_PROBE_SIZE` guards with code comments stating exactly why ("Views larger than this are left alone (parsing/annotating would be too slow)").
